Findings revealed no significant discrepancies in density or clustering but marked variability in spatial centrality. Furthermore, an analysis of research impact shows that authors in highly segregated communities gain more citations per paper when situated in peripheral areas, with a heightened probability of receiving citations from within their own community regardless of core position conversely, researchers from non-segregated contexts accumulate more citations in central and intermediate cores. To our current understanding, this research represents an original characterization of segregated communities and their impact on scientific citation metrics.

Traditionally, experts rely on native speakers to label popular benchmark datasets, a strategy that is often impractical for resources requiring recruitment for certain languages. Furthermore, unlike sampling the entire underlying DpP distribution itself, which would raise computational costs, our estimators simplify to sampling the necessary DpP linear statistics, streamlining implementation. Finally, extensive synthetic and on-real-data experiments corroborate these theoretical advancements.

We investigate the interplay between sorting algorithms and Binary Search Trees (BSTs) to reveal a deeper connection than currently recognized. Our analysis centers on the log-interleave bound (LIB), an information-theoretic measure quantifying a permutation's complexity. Under the framework of adaptive sorting—where lists are nearly ordered according to specific disorder metrics—the LIB aligns with the strongest known disorder measures. Interestingly, these disorder measures closely resemble established BST upper bounds like the dynamic finger bound and the work set bound, further hinting at the two fields' relationship. We provide three key findings on the LIB that strengthen these links. First, we prove the LIB remains within a $\lg \lg n$ multiplicative gap of a known BST lower bound; thus, any online BST algorithm matching the LIB's performance would equal the state-of-the-art $\lg \lg n$-competitive strategy. Second, we present a standalone BST algorithm that retrieves any entry of a permutation $\pi}$ using only $O(\mathrm{lib}(\pi) 
 accesses—a methodology that also generalizes the conversion of standard sorting algorithms into offline BST schemes. Finally, we offer a highly parallel merging sort algorithm designed for permutations whose total work adheres to the LIB criterion, contributing to advances in parallel BST execution.

Hypergraphs effectively represent multi-way interactions and have found widespread use in domains such as computer vision, higher-order network analysis, machine learning, and geometry processing. This paper establishes a theoretical framework for analyzing hypergraph spaces by leveraging principles from optimal transport. We achieve a general and resilient analysis of collective hypergraph structures by augmenting them with probability distributions across nodes and hyperedges, along with relational data encoding both local and global features. First, we define a distance metric for hypergraphs inspired by the co-optimal transport framework proposed by Redko et al. and investigate its mathematical properties. Secondly, we define mappings representing common strategies for converting hypergraphs into standard graphs, examining their functorial characteristics and establishing corresponding Lipschitz bounds within these spaces. Finally, the practical adaptability of our Hypergraph Co-Optimal Transport (HyperCOT) framework is illustrated through a variety of applications and examples.

Although Vision Transformers (ViTs) have gained widespread traction, their substantial computational expense poses significant challenges, primarily due to complexity increasing quadratically with input sequence length. Consequently, mainstream strategies focus on token reduction techniques ranging from progressive, structured spatial down-sampling to unstructured methods that dynamically prune redundant tokens. However, current approaches suffer from two critical drawbacks: the irregular spatial structures created by random pruning conflict with structured spatial hierarchies typical of deep, narrow models; and these methods often demand computationally intensive, data-centric pre-training. To address these issues and broaden token pruning's applicability, we introduce Evo-ViT, featuring a self-reflective slow-fast token refinement mechanism. This method leverages inherent, globally effective class-attention scores for unstructured instance-wise selection to identify informative tokens. Furthermore, we propose dual-potentiation update pathways—slow-fast updating—to distinguish how selected tokens and uninformative ones evolve. By preserving spatial continuity and data flow, Evo-ViT accelerates training for both flat and deep, narrow architectures from the initialization phase. Empirical validation confirms that this approach significantly diminishes computational costs while sustaining competitive image classification accuracy on standard benchmarks.

> Current practice typically favors parametric methods for the majority of task fMRI analyses, although these techniques rely on multiple specific assumptions. Although isolated components of fMRI models have previously been scrutinized, no study to date has comprehensively tested them using full empirical datasets. This research performed approximately two million randomized task fMRI group analyses on resting-state data to evaluate empirical familywise error rates for the packages FSL, AFNI, SPM, and a conventional non-parametric permutation approach. Although results varied slightly across contexts, at a nominal familywise error rate of 5%, parametric methods proved conservative for voxel-wise inference yet invalid for cluster-wise inference; notably, cluster size inference utilizing a cluster-forming threshold (CFT) of $p = 0.01$ resulted in inflated error rates of up to 60%. Further investigations indicate that this validity issue in cluster inference stems from spatial auto-correlation profiles failing to align with the assumed Gaussian form. Conversely, the non-parametric permutation test, resting on minimal assumptions, yielded valid outcomes for both voxel-wise and cluster-wise analyses. When compared using actual task data against a single parametric method, stark discrepancies emerged in the inferential conclusions derived through cluster analysis. Collectively, these insights underscore the necessity for rigorously validating the statistical tools employed throughout neuroimaging.

Federated learning (FL) represents an emerging machine learning field where a central server collaborates with numerous distributed clients, who contribute their private local datasets, to build a global model without personally disclosing the data. While standard FL addresses this, conventional approaches often suffer from significant hurdles such as heavy communication burdens and excessive strain on client resources. Existing research proposes various strategies to mitigate these problems, but this paper introduces a new "model growing" methodology. In this process, a low-complexity model is deployed on clients during training. As rounds progress and performance with this small model stagnates or saturates a specific level of data complexity handled by clients, a function-preserving expansion is initiated. During this stage of expanding model size to learn greater data patterns, the most robust and intricate model architecture is not introduced at the outset; instead, only the final version, possessing the desired efficacy but maximum complexity, is broadcast to clients, minimizing computational pressure. Extensive evaluations against three established datasets confirm that our approach achieves the theoretical benefits of FL efficiency, offering substantial reductions in communication volume and computational demand while maintaining predictive performance equivalent to leading current techniques.

This study examines data detection performance for complex values within massive MIMO frameworks. The central objective is to reconstruct an $n$-dimensional signal, where elements are sampled from a general constellation $\mathcal{K} \subset \mathbb{C}$, utilizing $m$ noisy linear observations and an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) complex Gaussian channel matrix. Because the ideal maximum likelihood (ML) detector remains computationally intractable for high dimensions, numerous convex relaxation heuristic approaches have been developed to tackle detection. We investigate a regularization extension of these methods, termed the regularized convex relaxation (RCR) detector, and explicitly establish asymptotic formulas for its mean squared error and symbol error rate. Finally, our theoretical findings are corroborated via Monte-Carlo simulations.

This research explores quantum metrology involving multiple copies of both bipartite and multipartite quantum states by evaluating their advantage relative to separable states and identifying a broad spectrum of entangled states that reach maximal utility when replicated infinitely fast. Our study also evaluates the utility derived from a lone sample of these entangled particles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain qubits containing multi-qubit states become operationally beneficial upon localization, even though they previously lacked utility. Finally, we analyze the implications for error-correction protocols and applications within noise-intolerant quantum information environments using this approach.

This study introduces a versatile framework for calculating a condensed version of the exponential of a high-dimensional function, denoted as $\exp(h)$). By discretizing this ODE with a Petrov–Galerkin scheme, we generate a structured solution via a Tensor Trains decomposition for which an efficient and robust a posteriori error estimator is developed. The PANOSETI (Panoramic SETI) experiment seeks to discover and measure optical transients across a wide field-of-view ($\sim$4,450 square degrees) with timing precision ranging from nanoseconds up to one second. To satisfy these demanding criteria for fast telemetry and extensive coverage, the project will deploy two telescope arrays, each containing approximately 45 units. Within these systems, custom-built fast photon-counting devices and ($f/1.32$) optical lenses work in parallel alongside a coincidence detection mechanism to screen against spurious signals. Data from a prototype setup consisting of two telescope pairs covering a 100-square-degree section is analyzed regarding functional performance and false positive frequency. Findings indicate that positioning synchronized telescopes for an identical field-of-view over a distance exceeding 1 kilometre markedly lowers the occurrence of local interference (such as Cherenkov light shows) compared to an adjacently located side-by-side formation. Additionally, reports outline the engineering parameters for the proposed all-sky instrument and projected coverage capabilities.

The paper introduces **DICHASUS**, a distributed massive MIMO channel sounder designed to capture extensive channel state information (CSI) datasets. Collected measurements hold potential applications in analyzing various machine learning techniques, ranging from user localization and joint cognitive access (JCAS) to channel cartography, alongside supporting dual-functional FDD massive MIMO operations, with other use cases possible. Uniquely, the proposed architecture features receivers with single-antennae that function completely autonomously, permitting entirely flexible, spatial distribution of antennas and providing virtually boundless scalability in antenna quantity. Addressing the prevalent yet insufficiently researched issue of localizing targets lying outside the convex hull of anchors in vehicle, UAV, and self-localizing contexts, this study optimizes anchor configurations for Time- of-Arrival (ToA) localization to minimize the maximum Dilution of Precision (DOP). Drawing on established asymptotic laws for DOP beyond the convex hull, we introduce a new Range-Normalized DOP (RNDOP). The analysis demonstrates that achieving worst-case DOP optimality reduces to solving an RNDOP min-max optimization. However, this specific formulation proves to be a challenging, intractable non-convex problem under typical constraints. To address this limitation, we introduce iterative anchor addition methods that convert the problem into a tractable form, albeit still non-convex. Capitalizing on the specific structure of the generated rank-1 updates, we formulate three heuristic approaches balanced against performance and computational costs. Furthermore, we establish theoretical upper and lower bounds regarding the optimization of worst-case 3D and 2D positioning errors. These theoretical findings serve as the basis for a generalized iterative framework designed for robust anchor placement, accompanied by an analysis of the proposed algorithms' computational demands. Finally, our theoretical predictions are verified through numerical experiments, alongside extensive Monte-Carlo simulations comparing positioning accuracy and processing times across the iterative methods; these results elucidate their performance trade-offs and offer critical design guidelines for systems operating beyond the convex hull.

We present a functional docking and navigation controller developed exclusively for the single-camera-equipped, autonomous John Deere Tango mower. Our purely vision-based approach is valuable due to its cost-efficiency, simplicity in deployment, and elimination of external sensors, distinguishing it from conventional systems that integrate global positioning system (GPS) data and position sensors. The object detection module identifies specific features on the mower and extracts a low-dimensional vector, allowing the RL network to learn efficiently the maneuvers required to maneuver the device into a desired location. This paper presents an approach designed to improve scalability in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) networks enhanced by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), specifically focusing on channel estimation. In the proposed algorithm, RIS reflection coefficient vectors are generated as a pre-existing offline library. For any selection from this library, only the overall end-to-end channel and corresponding transmit power distribution are estimated, thereby streamlining the search for the optimal reflection pattern by simply selecting the one that maximizes data rates within the pre-designed set. Unlike traditional methods lacking this flexibility, this technique allows the adaptation of training overhead based on the channel's coherence duration. Additionally, the study investigates the computational demands of this methodology and evaluates how achievable data rates scale with respect to the count of training slots underestimation assumptions; simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed framework significantly outperforms current solutions by minimizing both training overhead and computational burden while simultaneously enhancing performance even with channel estimation inaccuracies.

Supervised learning is increasingly applied in critical decision-making processes such as hiring, financial lending, and university admission. Unfortunately, models can inherit biases from their training data to discriminate against protected characteristics like race and gender. Beyond unfair treatment, concerns about data privacy emerge when models unintentionally disclose sensitive information. Although differential privacy is a prominent concept in addressing privacy risks, our work investigates its potential when paired with a differentially private exponential mechanism as a post-processing step. Unlike previous studies, our framework addresses selection tasks where a fixed, limited budget of positions exists, mirroring constraints common in college admission and professional hiring. While modern Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) can easily detect feasible remote application-layer attacks involving malicious packets, more subtle and potentially disruptive link-layer attacks have recently emerged, albeit with a traditional requirement for physical bus access. While quantum state overlap is the standard metric for comparing quantum states within classical frameworks, it fails to capture the intricate configurations of many-body systems. This insight reveals an ultimate quantum limit on the efficiency of converting physical resources into computational advantages.

Tested on the Argoverse benchmark, our model secures a first-place ranking and supersedes existing best results.

Veldkamp polygons are specific graphs, $\Gamma=(V,E)$, where a symmetric, anti-reflexive relation, $\equiv_v$, is assigned to each vertex $v\in V$. All such relations are trivial if and only if $\Gamma$ constitutes a thick generalized polygon. A Veldkamp polygon defined as flat possesses the characteristic that no two vertices share the identical set of opposites according to a natural definition. This study investigates the interplay between Veldkamp quadrangles and polar spaces to provide a complete classification of flat Veldkamp quadrangles featuring partially trivial relations, where $\equiv_v$ is applied only to a subset rather than all vertices of relations.

Although deep learning has gained significant traction in learning analytics over the past few years, real-world applications remain limited, partly owing to concerns about opacity and trust. This paper addresses this challenge by applying Explainable AI techniques to black-box neural networks, specifically within the domains of hybrid and online instruction for student outcome prediction. Employing a controlled study design involving multiple course pairs, we analyze how variations differ in one educational factor by examining two established instance-level interpretability tools: LIME and SHAP. Statistically, we measure the divergence between generated explanations across these courses and methods, while qualitatively we validate their utility through interviews with 26 academic experts. These researchers evaluated the models' identified feature contributions to student success, assessed their level of trust in the various explanations, and discussed strategies for applying these insights to improve course design. Key findings reveal substantial quantitative disagreement between explainers regarding feature importance and a lack of expert consensus on which outputs are most credible, regardless of the reliability involved during model training. Full access to results, interview scripts, and accompanying files is available via the project's GitHub repository.

Manufacturing sectors have increasingly utilized the recycling of machine components to cut expenses and promote sustainability. Identifying reusable attributes within part designs and matching them against similar entries in databases is a critical step. This project employs fully convolutional geometric features, leveraging inductive transfer learning to extract and learn high-level semantic characteristics from CAD models; their corresponding identical matches from a database are identified via the Frobenius norm. The retrieved performance was notably improved by feeding extracted features through a convolutional neural network augmented with spatial pyramid pooling. Results demonstrate that the proposed model efficiently captures the fundamental geometrical aspects of machine cutting features.

The open-domain dialogue system, Alquist, aspires to conduct conversations that are both coherent and engaging, representing a key metric of social intelligence. Developed during the fourth round of the Alexa Prize Socialbot Grand Challenge, the fourth iteration introduces two key innovations focusing on coherence and engagement. Regarding coherence, the proposed solution employs a new hybrid strategy integrating manually designed responses with generative modeling. This approach leverages handcrafted dialogue paths for high-quality interactions, utilizes out-of-topic detection to avoid nonsensical scripted replies when users deviate, and applies an automated response generator to creatively bridge the gap back toward structured conversational themes. For engagement, the innovations draw upon the principles of the exploration-exploitation balance; specifically, it balances learning a partner's interests through discovery (exploration) against applying known preferences to foster connection (exploitation). This work details the internal mechanics of Alquist, outlines the principles behind these advancements, and discusses the experimental results used to validate their performance.

Myocardial perfusion MRI analysis could rapidly deliver automated and operator-independent insights into heart ischemia. To address this, researchers employ Bayesian inference, which leverages prior knowledge to enhance parameter reliability; however, applying the time-demanding Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling required for approximate posterior distribution calculation is slow. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes leveraging convolutional neural networks, trained exclusively on labels generated by the Bayesian inference method. These networks learn to predict kinetic parameters derived from myocardium signal curves. Consequently, the result is drastically reduced computational time—enabling rapid predictions—without sacrificing accuracy compared to the original Bayesian model.

Our approach outperforms previous augmentation techniques and doubles the accuracy of state-of-the-art models—such as AtLoc and MapNet—under unprecedented challenging weather conditions.

This abstract presents an analysis of Higgs boson pair production (resonant and non-resonant) within the $b\bar{b}\tau^+\tau^-$ decay channel. By integrating structural context with semantics via non-Euclidean projections, HopfE preserves both high expressions. Extensive testing across established benchmarks confirms that HopfE leads a state-of-the-art performance for knowledge graph completion.

In combinatorial causal bandit (CB) systems, a learning agent intervenes on a subset of at most $K$ variables per round and gathers feedback with the primary objective of minimizing the expected regret on the outcome variable $Y$. This discussion focuses on binary generalized linear models (BGLMs) featuring a concise parametric representation of the underlying causal structure. We propose the BGLM-OFU algorithm for Markovian BGLMs, which assumes the absence of latent confounders and employs maximum likelihood estimation; theoretically, we demonstrate that it guarantees an expected regret scaling of $O(\sqrt{T}\log T)$ over a horizon of $T$. Addressing a more complex scenario involving hidden variables within the class of linear models, we leverage causal inference principles such as the do-calculus to transform the original model into an equivalent Markovian form. Consequently, we prove that our BGLM-OFU method—and an alternative approach rooted in linear regression—are both effective for handling linear causal structures that include latent confounding. The primary contributions of this work include: (a) extending research to cover combinatorial intervention sets and broader causal frameworks, potentially including those with hidden factors; (b) synthesizing and adapting methodologies from various domains, such as generalized linear bandit theory and online influence maximization; and (c) circumventing overly restrictive assumptions found in earlier literature, such as the necessity to know the conditional joint distribution of parents under all interventions, as well as eliminating the exponential dependence on causal graph dimensions that previously plagued regret analysis.

Using microwave spectroscopy, we directly observed the low-energy excitation modes in the quantum Ising magnet LiHoF\(_4\). Outlier detection, commonly referred to as anomaly or deviation detection, involves identifying data points that exhibit a significant difference from established patterns. In industrial settings, anomalies are frequent and often arise from sources like system failures, human errors, or fraud. While various methods have addressed these outliers, density-based strategies—notably the Local Outlier Factor (LOF) which is widely dominant—are increasingly favored, though their computational heft remains a significant drawback. To tackle efficiency issues related to LOF, this paper introduces a new pruning technique. This approach reduces computational overhead while sustaining detection performance through Prune-based LOF (PLOF). Unlike the original, this version initially calculates outlierness for all instances and only computes specific LOF scores for those surpassing certain thresholds. Experimental evaluation, supported by comprehensive comparisons between PLOF, standard LOF, and two modern variants, confirms the methodology's effectiveness: it achieves superior accuracy and precision with considerably faster execution times.

These strategies are built on specific assumptions regarding credibility transmission within different diffusion structures: one leverages the retweet network to trace how falsehoods move among accounts, a second utilizes the account-source bipartite network to target the credibility reliability of material posted by an account, and a third employs the news co-sharing network to analyze similarities between content disseminated by separate profiles. We implement multiple network centrality techniques and embedding algorithms to compute account credibility and subsequently evaluate this methodology systematically using empirical networks derived from Twitter data. Our findings indicate that extended versions of traditional centrality measures perform well for the reticket and account-source models, whereas embedding approaches excel when applied to retwitring or content-similarity contexts, achieving lower false positive detection at a computational price. However, these embedding methods come with higher computational complexities and reduced transparency compared to the centrality strategies used.

Estimation of translation quality plays an essential role in minimizing the effort required for post-editing in machine translations and in cleaning cross-lingual datasets. Quality estimation serves this purpose by predicting the fidelity of specific sentence pairs without relying on reference translations and simultaneously flagging areas requiring correction for human intervention. This paper introduces Verdi, a comprehensive model designed to assess word-level and sentence-level post-editing costs within parallel linguistic corpora. The architecture leverages two separate word predictors: a transformer-based neural machine translator and a cross-lingual language model, allowing it to derive varied discriminative features. By exploiting the inherent bidirectional nature of bilingual corpora, the NMT component employs a model-based dual-learning strategy. This task involves concurrently learning a direct translation task and its dual counterpart while sharing model parameters, resulting in superior predictive capabilities compared to unidirectional models. Utilizing this dual-learning setup enables an innovative feature that explicitly encodes the target language information, independent of the original context. Comprehensive evaluations using the WMT 2QE datasets demonstrate that this framework not only exceeds current benchmark record-holders but also outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches substantially. Additionally, the study successfully repurposes Verd's sentence-level scores to refine a bilingual corpus, resulting in measurable gains in both speech model performance and training efficiency.

Achieving optimal quality images through Plane-Wave Imaging (PWI) relies critically on the beamforming process. Adaptive techniques achieve this by determining apodization weights directly from the echoes collected by multiple transducer elements. This study formulates PWI beamforming within a framework of blind source separation, treating the signal output from individual transducer elements as non-independent field observations. By aiming to isolate an independent signal component from this set of data, the beamforming task is established and subsequently solved by adapting an Independent Component Analysis (ICA) algorithm for image reconstruction. The efficacy of this proposed method is assessed across datasets comprising computer simulations, real phantoms, and in vivo recordings from the Medical Imaging UW Ultrasound Group's plane-wave challenge, while also examining its performance under various imaging configurations compared to classical delay-and-sum beamformers. Notable improvements include a gain of up to 36.5% in lateral resolution and 10% in contrast relative to traditional approaches. Additionally, the authors benchmark the results against other standard adaptive techniques to highlight its advantages.

We introduce Prompt-and-Rerank, an approach to arbitrary textual style transfer (transforming text into a specified style) using general pre-trained language models. Built on a mathematical framework, the method breaks the task down into three distinct elements: textual similarity, target style adherence, and fluency. The process initially employs zero-shot or few-shot prompting to generate candidate sentences within the desired style, which are subsequently re-ordered based on the three metrics. Our empirical findings show that this approach allows smaller pre-trained models to match the performance of state-of-the-art large-scale architectures while utilizing significantly less computational power and memory (two orders of magnitude). Additionally, we perform a detailed analysis on seven diverse style transfer datasets, examining how model size and various prompt engineering strategies (such as prompt rewriting or delimiter selection) impact the quality of the resulting style transfer.

The cRPA method allows for the treatment of diverse excitation modes in the ($n,\gamma$) reaction, such as soft dipole modes, giant resonances, single-particle resonances, and non-collective excitations, while also accounting for low-lying surface vibrational states following the transition. Standard classification methods often underperform when tackling real-world data tainted by noisy labels. To address this, our paper introduces a variant of Gaussian Mixture Discriminant Analysis (GMDA) designed to handle noise specific to each label category. By incorporating flipping probabilities and class probabilities, and employing the EM algorithm to address the discriminant problem under these noisy conditions, our approach offers both a robust framework and rigorous proofs of convergence. Empirical evaluations across both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that this proposed method significantly outstrips performance compared to the other four cutting-edge solutions tested.

Network alignment, which seeks to identify significant correspondences between nodes in disparate graphs, is a crucial task in graph mining with wide-ranging applications. A cornerstone principle in this domain, Matched Neighborhood Consistency (MNC), dictates that nodes exhibiting similar structure or distance in one graph ought to map to corresponding proximate nodes in the other. We present a theoretical analysis establishing a strong linkage between MNC and alignment performance, noting that many conventional methods fail to maintain topological integrity across challenging instances. Consequently, we introduce a refinement approach called RefiNA, which enhances alignment solutions by better enforcing MNC, is easy to deploy, and scales effectively using sparse approximations to work alongside any existing unsupervised network alignment algorithm. Comprehensive evaluations reveal that RefiNA can improve alignment accuracy by as much as 90% and enable robust graph matching where topological differences span five times greater distances than previously handled.

Dynamic computed tomography perfusion (CTP) is a valuable noninvasive method for assessing and diagnosing acute ischemic stroke. This process generates hemodynamic parametric maps of the brain from sequential CT acquisitions during the initial passage of iodinated contrast. However, because repeated scanning results in high radiation exposure, clinical adoption necessitates reducing the dose; this reduction introduces noise that must be suppressed to maintain diagnostic reliability. This study presents a self-supervised deep learning algorithm specifically designed to denoise CTP, an approach that eliminates the requirement for high-dose reference images typically needed for training. The model functions by learning to estimate the characteristics of one frame from its neighboring frames; since source and target noises are statistically independent, theoretical analysis and simulation show this strategy is highly effective for noise removal. Crucially, avoiding the reliance on high-dose images streamlines the model's integration across varying scanning protocols and facility setups, allowing greater adaptivity. Validation using both simulation and public real-world datasets confirms that the proposed technique yields superior image quality, spatial resolution, and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) compared to traditional methods, even performing better than supervised approaches that were trained on simulated data rather than high-dose real data.

Numerical experiments across ten- and one-hundred-dimensional problems are included, which validate both theoretical predictions and demonstrate the high efficiency of the proposed approaches in handling dimensional scalability for parabolic equations.

Shock breakout represents the initial luminous signal from a supernova explosion, initially manifesting briefly as a UV flash under spherical symmetry. However, in axisymmetric and non-spherical prolate geometries, the shock wave first pierces the surface of the star along its symmetry axis and subsequently moves outward at wider angles, resulting in a light curve that can vary significantly from the standard spherical model. Our study investigates the emergence of a non-relativistic, bipolar shock originating from a spherical star to determine key characteristics of the resulting shock breakout. Depending on varying levels of asphericity, four distinct categories of breakout light curves can be identified. When compared to standard spherically symmetric events, significantly aspherical breakouts display two primary distinctions: they produce a longer but intrinsically fainter initial flash, followed by an extensive period of gradually declining or even rising emission caused by the expansion and cooling of ejected material launched at an angle via the oblique breakout. The flash duration is estimated to reach a maximum of approximately $R_*/v_{\rm bo}$, using the star's radius and the peak ejecta velocity respectively; for a typical Wolf--Rayet progenitor, the longer-than-anticipated prompt X-rays detected in SN 2008D and similar events to GRB 060218 violate this threshold. Such observations suggest that these phenomena do not result from axisymmetrical disturbances typical of a regular Wolf--Rayet core, but originate instead from unique, non-standard progenitors capable of larger breakout radii.

The primary goal of this research is to develop improved variations of the Euler method incorporating adaptive interpolation using both inverse-quadratic and multi- quadratic radial basis functions (RBF) for solving initial value problems. These enhanced algorithms increase the convergence rate locally by leveraging the free parameter inherent in RBF models. To substantiate the findings, rigorous consistency, convergence, and stability analyses are conducted. Numerical experiments confirm that the achieved accuracy and convergence speeds match or surpass those of the original Euler method, particularly as they are able to eliminate local truncation error, thereby demonstrating that these adaptive approaches are optimal.

Citation counts are a widespread metric for evaluating scientific work, yet their value depends on factors beyond quality alone, including conventionality, team size, and author gender. This study investigates how a paper's degree of conventionality correlates with its citation percentile within a specific field using a developed metric called "topic disparity," defined as the cosine distance between the paper and the dominant discipline within a neural embedding space. We demonstrate that higher topic disparity—which indicates divergence from the norm—is associated with lower citation percentiles in numerous disciplines, regardless of team size and the genders of the principal authors. This suggests that less conventional research tends to garner fewer citations than more standard work. Furthermore, our proposed method aids in supplementing traditional raw citation data by helping identify significant contributions on the fringes of established disciplines due to their innovative topics.

Global climate change has severely damaged the environment, and prior research has linked the resulting pest disasters to mass tree die-off, which inevitably increases the risk of forest fires—a phenomenon closely tied to overall forest health status. Aerial imagery provides a capability for detecting dead versus healthy trees. This paper introduces a novel, automated framework for dead tree identification from aerial photos using Mask RCNN, enhanced by a reconstruction technique for data augmentation and implemented through transfer learning by comparing eight fine-tuned model variants using our specific imagery dataset. This approach allows for automatic generation and calculation of dead-tree instance masks (achieving an optimal mean average precision of 54%), thereby establishing a direct measure of forest health useful for investigating the anthropocentric drivers of fire hazards associated with changing climatic conditions.

The Hausdorff distance is a standard metric for assessing both the similarity and dissimilarity between two sets, widely employed across numerous fields. Although the majority of applied research focuses on calculating this metric for finite collections of points—such as those in image processing—we aim to apply the Hausdorff distance to control and evaluate optimisation techniques within level-set based shape optimisation. In such cases, the entities being compared are characteristically level-sets or defined via signed distance functions rather than finite point sets. Consequently, this paper investigates methods for computing the Hausdorff distance between these non-geometra types. We begin by reviewing fundamental properties of the metric, particularly its formulation in terms of distance functions. For numerical contexts, this formulation provides at least an exact lower bound on the distance. Furthermore, we derive a complementary upper bound, which enables the construction of precise error estimates supported by a practical example proving that no further generic reduction of these errors is possible in the worst-case scenario. However, we also demonstrate that error accuracy can improve significantly under typical, non-pathological conditions usually found in application settings. Additionally, the proposed error estimate can be further enhanced if the underlying grid is rotated randomly relative to the shapes involved.

Biofilms create significant challenges across engineering domains, including biomedicine, bioenergy, and marine science, making their effective control a critical long-term objective. Crucial to both the formation and removal of biofilms are their adhesion andSurface mechanics. Custom-designed nano-surfaces featuring varying topologies can modify these adhesive properties, thereby facilitating easier elimination of biofilms and substantially enhancing long-term control strategies. To accelerate the development of such topologies, we utilized individual-based modeling combined with Bayesian optimization, creating an automated process for generating distinct functional surfaces aimed at effective biofilm remediation. Our framework proved successful in producing optimal nano-surfaces for eliminating biofilms through applied viscous shear and vibration. Our analysis identified a densely packed arrangement of short pillars as the most effective geometry for preventing biofilm adhesion. Conversely, when subjected to fluid shear, a sparse configuration of tall, slender pillar-like structures was optimal. For scenarios involving vertical or lateral vibration control, thick trapezoidal cones emerged as the best-suited morphology. Furthermore, optimizing vibrational parameters revealed that low-frequency vibrations applied with small magnifications achieve superior biofilm removal efficiency. Ultimately, these findings offer valuable insights for multiple engineering sectors requiring surface-mediated biofilm management; additionally, this framework is adaptable for generalizing material design and optimization efforts.

This work establishes a near-horizon soft gluon theorem for the Schwarzschild black hole, deriving it from the Ward identity associated with near-horizon large gauge transformations. The soft gluon theorem defined in flat spacetime emerges as a specific limit within this curved spacetime framework.

The study establishes fractional Sobolev-Poincaré inequalities, capacity-based fractional Poincaré inequalities, as well as pointwise and localized fractional Hardy inequalities within a metric space featuring a doubling measure. These findings generalize and extend previous work focused on non-fractional settings in metric spaces or on fractional cases in Euclidean spaces. Notably, the new pointwise and localized versions of the Hardy inequalities hold true even for the classical Euclidean framework, marking a distinct advancement.

Scientific research is increasingly shifting toward a data-centric model where AI-driven computations applied to domain-specific large-scale data generate discoveries. Contemporary machine learning tools make it possible for anyone to build and run algorithms uncovering latent data insights for scientific applications. However, evaluating every feasible algorithm across major, resource-intensive datasets is economically impossible due to the prohibitive cloud compute costs associated with such tasks. Current practical benchmarks circumvent this by inferring results from smaller, representative sets, yet this restricts the number of datasets profiled comprehensively and biases outcomes in favor of methods optimized for generic cases. Consequently, distinct dataset features remain unexamined, often yielding the selection of underperforming algorithms based on overly general proxies. These challenges demand a reimagined methodology integrating dataset profiling directly into model selection. To justify a dataset-specific profiling approach, we address two critical inquiries: First, do scientific datasets fundamentally reorder the ranking of computational models compared to standard benchmarks? Second, if deviations do occur, would executing lightweight trials enhance benchmarking precision? Together, responding to these questions establishes the foundation for a novel benchmarking paradigm attuned to dataset specificity.

Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites are a fundamental requirement for equal-access networking thanks to their combination of high capacity, low signal latency, and uninterrupted global reach. The discussion further examines how variables such as gateway density and satellite counts and orbital altitudes affect both latency and coverage success rates. Ultimately, the article concludes with projections for future SG applications.

To alleviate risks from adverse weather, meteorological authorities disseminate public weather warnings based primarily on outputs from predictive models. Selecting an appropriate system or combination of systems for warning purposes necessitates comparing their capacities to accurately forecast the frequency and intensity of severe weather. Nonetheless, assessing forecasts for such extreme events poses significant challenges, a problem intensified by complex confounding factors in high-impact precipitation that have spurred substantial inquiry into compound weather events. Consequently, both univariate and multivariate approaches are needed for evaluation. This paper explores weighted verification tools that prioritize specific outcomes during scoring assessments. It reviews and contrasts various methods for constructing weighted scoring rules across univariate and multivariate frameworks, extending foundational work on weighted probabilities into new weighted probability integral transform (PIT) histograms to conditionally verify forecast calibration. A case study utilizing MeteoSwiss forecasts for extreme heat demonstrates the practical value of these specialized verification tools.

Precise and rapid simulation of particle interactions is essential for the high-energy physics community, yet emulating these processes with detectors remains time-consuming and computationally demanding. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC), operating with 13 TeV proton-proton collisions, offers a unique capability to observe and quantify rare phenomena that could redefine our understanding of new physical interactions. However, the ongoing upgrade toward the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) will overwhelm current infrastructure with increased data loads from higher event rates and significant pile-up. To support HL-LHC, simulations must achieve substantial speedups without compromising physics accuracy. This discussion highlights how machine learning techniques can provide efficient alternatives that maintain high fidelity. Specifically, we present a graph generative model that delivers effective event reconstruction, establishing a foundation for complete detector-level fast simulation capable of addressing HL-LHC demands.

Topological insulators, Chern insulators, and Quantum Hall insulator phases are foundational models for understanding symmetry-protected topological states. This paper details the successful creation, in bilayer graphene and monolayer WSe$_2$ heterostructures, of the elusive yet pivotal topologically trivial-to-nontrivial intermediate phase featuring time-reversal invariant helical edge modes, a state known to precede generic topological insulator research. Our success in isolating this phase hinged on fabricating mesoscale systems integrating both a moiré superlattice potential and substantial spin-orbit coupling. This engineering yielded materials capable, via an external displacement field, of transitioning between trivial metallic and topologically active states. Our findings characterize the resulting topological phase as possessing a band bulk gap coupled with helical edge modes that exhibit conductive quantization precisely at $2e^2/h$, even in the absence of an external magnetic field. Grounded in corroborating experiments—including validation of the Landauer-Buttiker model predictions for multi-terminal quantum transport—our non-local transport measurements confirm these edge modes propagate dissipationlessly and maintain thermal equilibrium at contact points. By manipulating the phase topology using both electric and magnetic fields, we demonstrated transitions between a trivial state and several distinct nontrivial topological configurations. Accompanying these observations is a theoretical analysis of an realistic model that not only mirrors the observed phenomena but also clarifies the mechanisms underlying the bulk insulation and helical edges. Collectively, these combined insights outline a dependable experimental pathway toward the realization of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ time-reversal invariant topological phase.

We offer a proof-of-concept illustration of free-space quantum key distribution using single photons produced by an isolated defect within hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). Functioning at room temperature, the source, which yields 10% brightness per photon, utilizes the B92 protocol to achieve a secure key rate of 238 bits per second at 1 MHz and records 8.95% quantum error rate. Additionally, the analysis examines how adjusting the temporal filtering of detection affects QKD system performance, and we posit these findings will drive advancements in hBN's optically active defect capabilities and their integration into rigorous practical QKD applications.

Geo Knowledge graphs represent a robust, logic-based method for interconnecting entities through data reasoning that generates insights. However, when constructing these structures, modeling disaster events is typically restricted to individual, unconnected incidents, often overlooking the connections between successive, overlapping occurrences. This study proposes GeoArtificial Intelligence methodologies capable of discerning causal links, specifically for disaster events, by employing spatially and temporally constrained semantic rules. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a use case focused on cause-and-effect disaster modeling demonstrated that combining thematic identification of related incidents, spatiotemporal overlap constraints, and text-based analysis of event descriptions automates the detection of causality between separate events. Ultimately, our framework enriches event knowledge repositories and facilitates the investigation of chained event patterns within vast knowledge graphs, thereby enhancing query efficiency and discovery capabilities.

Let $\mathbf{P}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_k$ represent specific partial orders (posets). The {em Boolean Ramsey number}, denoted $R(\mathbf{P}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_k)$, refers to the minimum integer $n$ where every possible $k$-coloring of the Boolean lattice $\mathbf{B}_n$ guarantees the existence of at least one copy of $\mathbf{P}_i$ entirely colored with color $i$. Originally introduced by Axenovich and Walzer~\cite{AW}, this concept has recently yielded significant findings, particularly regarding cases where $\mathbf{P}_i$ are Boolean lattices themselves. This work focuses specifically on determining $R(\mathbf{P}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_k)$ when each $\mathbf{P}_i$ forms a "$V$-shaped" poset—a structure constructed by joining the minimal elements of two chains. A key outcome of the paper identifies the minimal such posets embedded within $\mathbf{B}_n$ that satisfy the Ramsey conditions once the value $R$ is established. The text further constructs another concept, the {\em Boolean rainbow Ramsey number}, $RR(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{Q})$, defined as the lowest $n$ ensuring any coloring of $\mathbf{B}_n$ produces either a monochromatic instance of $\mathbf{P}$ or a completely multi-colored (rainbow) instance of $\mathbf{Q}$. Previous work by Chang, Li, Gerbner, and their colleagues provided upper bounds for $RR(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{A}_k)$ involving general posets and the antichain $\mathbf{A}_k$. This article similarly investigates these bounds for scenarios where $\mathbf{P}$ is $V$-shaped.

Amidst the proliferation of big data and the Internet of Things, disseminating extensive datasets within insecure settings forces data owners into a dilemma balancing user privacy against data usefulness. While a mutual-information-driven privacy funnel has traditionally mediated this trade-off, it is often impractical due to difficulties in precisely quantifying mutual information when sample sizes are limited or underlying distribution functions are undefined. Addressing this gap, this work introduces a mutual-information-based privacy funnel that leverages the Mutual Information Neural Estimator (MINE) to refine the optimization balance. By abandoning traditional calculation methods in favor of a neural network-based training process, MINE generates a meticulously precise approximation. In the optimization framework, this estimated mutual information is deployed to regulate data retention and gauge privacy; the system then trains the network to maximize utility provided that the privacy disclosure metric stays beneath a specific limit. Empirical simulations confirm the efficacy of MINE in approximates mutual information accurately despite sparse data, effectively serving to measure both privacy leakage and utility preservation while optimizing their inherent trade-off.

This work presents a unified framework for generic video annotation utilizing bounding boxes. Given that video annotation is a burdensome and resource-intensive task, our solution addresses two significant hurdles: (1) automatically determining bounding box trajectories through both temporal interpolation and extrapolation for human-labeled frames not covered, and (2) autonomously identifying the most valuable frames to label by hand. Our contributions are twofold: firstly, a model capable of simultaneous interpolation and extrapolation; and secondarily, a guidance mechanism that iteratively suggests subsequent annotation frames based on prior work. We conduct comprehensive experiments across several complex datasets via simulation, demonstrating a 60% reduction in manual bounding box requirements relative to linear interpolation, and a 35% reduction over a standard off-the-shelf tracker. Our method also achieves a 10% speedup in annotation time compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, through human annotation trials with detailed result analysis, we reveal that the approach cuts actual annotation time by 50% when compared against typical linear interpolation techniques.

In various Machine Learning domains, selecting an appropriate kernel function for Gaussian Processes (GP)—an advanced method for regression and classification—is pivotal, as the technique's performance inherently depends on them. However, previous GP studies have typically relied on manually constructed kernels, choices from predefined collections, or searches within fixated composition spaces. This study introduces a genetic-programming algorithm that formulates kernel functions as structures composed of elementary mathematical operations defined within a tree. By enabling this representation, we broaden the designable kernel family to discover higher-potential solutions while introducing specific technical complexities, which the proposed method successfully addresses. The algorithms have proven capable of deriving kernels that perfectly reflect underlying data patterns, and when evaluated against real-time forecasting challenges, this approach not only outperforms existing standards but does so with reduced structural intricacy.

Staying informed of the latest trends, technologies, and established practices in visualization and data analytics presents a growing challenge, particularly for emerging data scientists. To address this issue, we introduce Lodestar, an interoper computational notebook framework enabling the rapid development and investigation of new data workflows by providing access to auto-generated analysis suggestions. Our methodology derives recommendations from directional event graphs of known workflows rooted in two datasets: manually curated content derived from online tutorials and analysis derived from semi-automatic scanning of a repository exceeding 6,000 Jupyter notebooks. A pilot evaluation informed a future roadmap of system enhancements, and findings indicate that users regard Lodestar as a beneficial tool for swiftly constructing data science pipelines.

Largely due to ongoing studies on image classification, there has been significant progress in optimizing training and inference efficiency. Understanding that many-body interactions depend closely on spatial dimension is essential to explaining many emergent quantum effects. A definitive manifestation is found in Bose gases confined to one dimension, where an abundance of conservation laws prevents thermal equilibrium and strictly limits how dynamics evolve. In our work, we reveal that such restrictive 1D characteristics can survive well into the intermediate 3D regime. We achieved this by taking a weakly interacting Bose trapped in an elongated potential, inducing the time evolution of a specific density component through a quantum quench. Applying the theoretical framework of Generalized Hydrodynamics, we found that the primary driver for relaxation was the 1D dephasing of the system's collective excitations, known as rapidities. Remarkably, this dephasing dominated even at temperatures far beyond where thermalization is typically expected in 1D. We attribute this finding to an emergent phenomenon akin to Pauli blocking affecting 3D excitations, driven by the fact that rapidities obey fermionic statistics even though the constituent gas particles are strictly bosonic. Therefore, we contend that the principles underlying 1D physics are more robust against perturbations than currently believed. Furthermore, utilizing exact Bethe ansatz solutions to model the complex many-body system enhances our comprehension of how macroscopic behaviors arise from their foundational microscopic properties.

A multitude of malware detectors, both commercial and based on open-source, currently exist. Yet their effectiveness is undermined by emerging adversarial attacks, such as feature-space manipulation designed to bypass identification. To address this, we have established a model-agnostic, explainability-focused framework that evaluates how well these detectors withstand adversarial threats. At its core, this approach introduces the Accrued Malicious Magnitude (AMM), a metric pinpointing specific malware features whose manipulation would most likely facilitate evasion. Using this method, we assessed various state-of-the-art detectors against artificially altered malware samples. Our analysis revealed that (i) major commercial anti-virus systems face vulnerabilities when confronting samples manipulated based on AMM guidance; (ii) the cross-detector evasion success (transferability) relies on the convergence of high AMM values across feature sets of competing detectors; and (iii) AMM scores successfully quantify feature significance and clarify evasion mechanisms. Ultimately, these results illuminate existing deficiencies in current detection systems and outline potential pathways for their enhancement.

Exponential-family random graph models (ERGMs) are probabilistic network frameworks defined through parameter sets that utilize sufficient statistics derived from structural, graph-theoretic characteristics. Within the R statistical computing environment, the `ergm` package offers various tools for conducting analysis under the ERGM paradigm. While the existing terms in this package allow for numerous network properties to serve as sufficient statistics for ERGMs, its capabilities can be extended to code additional network statistics via custom packages. This discussion centers specifically on introducing statistics derived from graphlets—small, connected, non-isomorphic induced subgraphs that encapsulate the topological arrangement of a network. To this end, the `ergm.graphlets` package for R has been developed, enabling the integration of graphlet properties directly into the `ergm` framework. Offering a comprehensive suite of model terms for 2-, 3-, 4-, and 5-node graphlets, the `ergm.graphlets` package facilitates both the structural modeling of global network features and the exploration of connections between nodal covariates and local network topologies.

It is theorized that oscillatory synchrony facilitates information transfer among brain regions, with specific phase-locked configurations enabling unique effective connections. Previous research suggests that multistable phase-locking allows hardwired brain networks to flexibly support various functional patterns without altering their structural wiring. Considering the proposed relationship between interregion communication and phase-locked states, it is crucial to understand how these states can be manipulated to rapidly modify functional connectivity in interregion circuits. This study examines the control of functional states in small, deterministically multistable networks of coupled neural masses, which additionally exhibit stochastic irregular oscillations and transient phase-locking. Specifically, we analyzed the global responses of these mesoscale circuits to external inputs directed at individual subcomponents. With a primary focus on realistic stochastic scenarios, we determined conditions where local inputs can (i) induce fast, transient transitions to topologically distinct connectivity motifs ("state switching"); (ii) gradually reconfigure the spatial pattern of phase relationships for specific lead-lag arrangements ("state morphing"); and (i) fail to control global locking states. Collectively, our findings contribute to emerging evidence indicating that modulating coherent multimodal patterns may serve as a foundation for flexible brain network functioning.

Emergency vehicles (EMVs) are critical in responding to urgent urban incidents, such as fires and medical crises, where minimizing travel time is vital for saving lives and protecting property. Existing solutions often rely on route optimization using historical traffic data combined with automatic traffic signal prioritization. A key limitation of these methods is the circular dependency created: signal prioritization dynamically shifts traffic flows, thereby altering the previously calculated optimal route. Furthermore, prioritizing EMVs frequently disrupts overall traffic stability and increases delays for other vehicles. This paper introduces EMVLight, a decentralized reinforcement learning framework capable of performing simultaneous dynamic routing and signal control. By extending Dijkstra's algorithm to instantly recalculate routes, EMVLight adapt guides emergency vehicles through the network in real time. The system utilizes decentralized RL agents trained on cooperative phase strategies that concurrently reduce travel durations for EMVs and mitigate average delay across the entire traffic network. Validated through rigorous experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets, EMVLight surpasses current traditional engineering benchmarks and other supervised reinforcement learning techniques.

This study provides a theoretical analysis of splitting two-ion crystals within segmented Paul traps, examining the shift from a shared confinement zone to individual separated traps. The instability ultimately drives the fragmentation of the uniform condensate, subsequently leading to a dynamic coarsening process where discrete quantum droplets amalgamate, thereby precipitating a rapid reduction in droplet population; numerical evaluations of the rate at which droplet numbers decline are performed for various initial setup conditions.

The phenomenon where molecular transitions strongly interact with photon fields results in hybrid light-matter excitations known as polaritons. While employing collective vibrational strong coupling to regulate chemical reactions holds significant potential, its efficacy is often hindered by an excess of nearly degenerate dark modes. This study investigates scattering exponents resulting from small-angle scattering off power-law polydisperse surface and mass fractals. We demonstrate that an aggregate of fractals with sizes governed by a power-law can exhibit an effective change in fractal dimension if its exponent reaches a sufficiently high magnitude; specifically, the new characteristic scattering dimension emerges due to spatial correlations between the locations of distinct fractals. However, at high values of momentum transfer, the influence of spatial correlations vanishes, meaning the resulting scattering intensity is simply a sum of the contributions from each component fractal separately. We have also determined the governing limitations on these power-law exponents, deriving results that extend and generalize Martin's formulas for the scattering exponents of polydisperse fractals.

The Rydberg blockade effect has recently facilitated the realization of quantum spin liquid states on the kagome lattice, with direct measurements of non-local string order confirming the presence of spin liquid behavior in those experimental results. This study introduces a BCS-type variational wave function to characterize this specific spin liquid state. This approach is inspired by mapping the Rydberg blockade system to a lattice gauge theory, wherein local gauge conservation laws assume the role typically filled by Ryd Blokade constraints. Using the experimentally measured Rydberg atom population, we calculate the corresponding variational parameters, generating a fully determined wave function which we then benchmark against experimental non-local string order data. Specifically, by combining data on open and closed strings and isolating fluctuations from closed loops as signatures of topological order, we demonstrate that this parameter-free predictive wave function aligns commendably well with empirical observations, offered one simple and intuitive picture for interpreting quantum spin liquid dynamics that can be extended to various model extensions.

Utilizing relativistic mean field theory, we examine how dark matter (DM) impacts the neutron equation of state (EoS) and star structure in scenarios both with and without a crust. By incorporating a WIMP-DM component into a $\sigma$-$\omega$ model that couples to nuclear matter via the Higgs portal, we find that our approach yields results comparable to studies using complex nucear models or advanced Higgs potential terms; specifically, DM softens the EoS and produces stars with reduced maximum mass. Conversely, the DM-modified EoS exhibits instabilities characterized by negative pressure at low-energy densities in the DM phase, a trend that intensifies as the DM Fermi momentum increases. To address this, we restrict the DM to the star's core. Furthermore, we replace the instability regions with three sequential crust models based on ideal gas, the Skyrm-Pandharipande-Skrone, and Srym-Lyön EoSs, and correspond an observed overall increase in radius with the mass of the neutron star to these changes.

This analysis reveals that including these types of cores allows for the stabilization of the DM-intermixed EoS and improves the understanding of the neutron star structure.

Dispersion characteristics of elastic waveguides feature instances where the group velocity drops to zero while the wavenumber remains finite; these locations are known as zero-group-velocity (ZGV) points. Because elastic energy persists near the source at these points without dissipating widely, they hold significant practical value for quantitative structural analysis and nondestructive evaluation, necessitating highly accurate prediction methods. This work initially addresses modeling anisotropic plates, deriving resonances via an exceptional mode phenomenon, and casts the fundamental equation as a two-parameter eigenvalue problem. Subsequently, we outline three compatible numerical strategies for calculating ZGV frequencies within arbitrary lossless elastic guides. The first approach offers global convergence ensuring the detection of every ZGV point, albeit limited to minor-scale problems. The second utilizes rapid, locally convergent Newton-type iteration applicable to general cases without global guarantee. Finally, we present a third integrally combined technique tailored for broad or large datasets that does not demand specific starting guesses but is still likely to capture the full set of ZGV points with high comprehensiveness in results.

We address multi-agent, episodic reinforcement learning by aiming to generate a policy that ensures social fairness among stakeholders possessing distinct reward functions. Previous literature has suggested optimization targets such as minimum and generalized Gini welfare for defining fair policies. This work begins with an axiomatic framework, introducing four conditions any fair policy objective should satisfy. We demonstrate that Nash social welfare is the sole objective satisfying all four axioms, while earlier approaches fail under this rigorous criteria. Shifting to the scenario with unknown dynamics (specifically unknown MDPs), we explore regret-minimization relative to three fair objectives: minimum welfare, generalized Gini welfare, and Nash social welfare. Leveraging optimism-based planning, we introduce a universal learning algorithm and provide corresponding regret bounds for agents pursuing these different fairness goals. Specifically, for the Nash objective, we establish a theoretical lower bound on regret that scales exponentially with the number of agents \(n\). In conclusion, we observe that within the scope of minimum welfare optimization, a weaker regret definition enables performance improvements of \(O(H) \times\).

This study focuses on light propagation within the context of three-dimensional electrodynamics. Specifically, it analyzes light ray behavior in a continuous, hypothetical bi-dimensional medium situated within a three-dimensional surrounding spacetime, employing a strictly covariant methodology. By assuming a local linear response tensor that links field strengths to inductions in this medium, we apply the principles of geometric optics to derive Fresnel's equation and utilize algebraic geometry theories to establish an effective optical metric.

Early neurobiological models of spatial cognition relied on data collected from constrained, simple environments rather than natural settings, leaving it unclear how to scale these theoretical models to complex spaces. Meanwhile, autonomous systems technology has increasingly focused on distributed control strategies capable of managing vast numbers of lightweight mobile units. Given that both animal groups and swarms of robots must navigate intricate, uncertain environments, we present the "NeuroSwarms" control framework to test if adopting neural circuit patterns from mammalian spatial cognition allows for adaptive, autonomous control in minimal agent-based swarms. In Neusworms, individual agents function as neurons and the group mimics a recurrent network: visible agents act like reciprocal attractor place cells via phase-state oscillations synchronized at theta rhythmic frequencies similar to hippocampal models. We show that multi-agent interactions and approach behaviors constitute a fluid application of Hebbian learning, aligning with established animal cognitive theories without requiring a single-entity framework. The framework generates complex emergence behaviors, such as phase-synchronized ring clusters and interaction sequences within environmental geometric cues inside extensive, fractured mazes. Ultimately, Neusworms serves as an artificial system bridging theoretical neuroscience and autonomous control to identify unifying principles advancing both fields.

This initiative served as the foundational step for the "Einstein-First" collaboration, aiming to challenge the prevailing paradigm centered exclusively on Newtonian physics in educational settings, demonstrating that upper primary students can indeed engage with material previously deemed too advanced for their age. 

To assess lasting efficacy, researchers conducted interviews and surveys in 2020 with a subgroup of eleven participants from the original cohort (having been part of a total 16). Furthermore, participants noted that the instructional analogies and models used over the intervention's six-week duration were vividly memorable, facilitating year-round recall. Crucially, more than ten years after the intervention occurred, participants retained several fundamental concepts, including those regarding curved space-time. 

This follow-up conclusively demonstrates that Einsteinian physics concepts are not only effectively instructional at an upper primary level but can also endure as lasting knowledge years after being taught in a primary classroom.

The inclusion of right-handed neutrinos (RHNs) extends the Standard Model, a move strongly supported by observed neutrino oscillations. Typically, within the type-I seesaw framework, RHN discovery is hamstrung at colliders because RHNs are only weakly correlated with active SM particles through minimal neutrino mixings. This research, however, adopts the type-I seesaw model but enhances it with a new leptoquark (LQ). We utilize an LQ-mediated, production pathway for the RHN that does not suffer suppression from these mixings. Our focus is on the discovery potential at the upcoming Large Hadron electron Collider (LHeC), assuming an LQ mass of 1 TeV and a lighter-scale RHN mass around the GeV level. In this regime, and given specific coupling values, produced RHNs are both sufficiently boosted from the LQ decay source and long-lived, yielding collimated decay products that form the distinctive signature we study: displaced fat jets. By analyzing event kinematics to isolate signal against background processes, we demonstrate that specific kinematic ratio variables, particularly those involving the displacement count or properties of the fat jets versus energy or displaced prompt tracks to total, effectively distinguish true displaced RHN decays. Additionally, we show that utilizing a positively electron beam for the experiment increases the sensitivity to detecting this signature by roughly an order of magnitude.

Measuring Inter-beat intervals (IBIs) facilitates heart-rate variability (HRV) estimation, offering a potential early warning for various cardiovascular conditions. However, deriving IBIs is difficult when signals are noisy due to distortion of their morphological shape; this issue is acute in Electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings from highly mobile individuals plagued by motion artifacts, resulting in inaccurate IBI data. Consequently, restoring ECG quality and accurately calculating IBIs have become focal points within remote health monitoring and wearable technology, particularly within the field of signal processing. While conventional methods remain in use, recent studies have shown that deep-learning approaches are highly effective for denoising, simplifying the diagnosis process and achieving previously unreachable accuracy. In our work, we introduce a deep-learning approach using a Tiramisu Autoencoder to mitigate motion artifacts, ensuring R-peak clarity in both clean and severely contaminated high-intensity motion scenarios. By denoising the signal, we achieve more precise IBI estimation, thus accelerating clinical tasks. Experiments demonstrate proficiency in estimating IBI from signals with a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) as low as -30dB, yielding a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) averaging only 13ms; at these noise levels of inaccuracy is confined beneath under 8% while surpassing current state-of-the-art techniques.

Next, we address scenarios with broken symmetries and non-conserved charges, offering a toy representation of global symmetry breaking during evaporation. Even within this basic framework, the symmetry-resolved entropies reveal various interesting aspects of the black hole-like evolutionary process.

By incorporating sophisticated learning techniques, LiBrE is rendered effective and efficient for detection purposes; specifically, we implement few-shot ensemble variance and leverage combined pre-training and fine-tuning regimes to enhance performance. While human understanding evolves in tandem with the underlying ideas, modern artificial agents employ the Abduction, Belief Revision, and Conceptual Change (ABC) repair system to adjust logical frameworks for such cognitive shifts. Unlike repair approaches that alter only membership rulings (such as defining which species can fly), this study targets the modification of the logical concepts themselves by restructuring the signatures of the theories they represent. We introduce a technique to automatically compute entrenchment within the signatures of Datalog-based logical theories to steer repair mechanisms toward outputs that are concise and intuitively sound, where entrenchment reflects the inferential significance of predicates and arguments. Recognized as a pliminary measure to contrast human judgment, evaluating which predicates are more entrenched allows the system to discard redundant alternatives and favor the most logical modifications for representing knowledge about conceptual change.

We introduce a monolithic second-order method tailored for simulating incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on irregular terrains using quadtree discretization. Employing a semi-collocated arrangement positions velocity values at vertex points and pressure variables within cell cores. Car sharing serves as a cornerstone of smart transportation systems, promising to alleviate urban traffic congestion, lower parking needs, and cut pollution. Over recent years, modeling efforts have expanded substantially from the molecular scale down to atomic and quantum levels. Computational chemistry serves a vital role by creating simulation models for systems, spanning from individual atoms to large industrial processes. Progress in computing power and algorithmic efficiency are key drivers influencing this field. The ability to represent chemical reactions through the theoretical lens of thermodynamics and classical automata theory has also made significant waves within the computer science community. A primary objective is therefore to investigate chemical information processing utilizing quantum computational frameworks. In this study, we develop two-way quantum finite automata to model chemical reactions, ensuring execution stops in linear time. Beyond this, we design classical pushdown automata to handle such reactions by using multiple stacks.
