A prevailing trend in recent generative modeling involves constructing 3D-aware synthesizers directly from collections of 2D images. While traditional methods often rely on volumetric rendering to enforce 3D consistency—though this becomes increasingly costly at high resolutions—a wave of over ten recent studies has attempted to address scalability by pairing a basic 3D generator with a distinct 2D decoder that upsamples either an intermediate low-res image or feature map. However, this hybrid strategy entails significant trade-offs, specifically compromising multi-view consistency (where shape and textures vary inconsistently across camera angles) and reconstructing geometry at low fidelity. Conversely, this paper proposes that high-resolution 3D generation with state-of-the-art image quality can be achieved by training purely via a patch-wise strategy, presented in a refined manner. We enhance two critical aspects of this optimization pipeline: first by introducing an adaptive, multi-spatial discriminator sensitive to location and scale, operating on patches of varying proportions and positions, and second by adjusting the patch sampling technique through an annealed beta distribution to boost training stability and speed. The resulting model, "EpiGRAF," offers an efficient solution for high-resolution, constraint-free 3D generation. Evaluated on four datasets—including two new ones added herein—at $512 \times 2$ and ${51}2\times{256}^2$ resolution—the architecture achieves SotA perceptual quality and geometric detail while training approximately two and a half times faster than approaches utilizing external upsamplers. Federated learning (FL) empowers multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine learning model while preventing any participant from exposing their raw data to others. Furthermore, since Fl is pseudolabel-based, it serves as a natural addition, particularly when paired with consistency-based approaches. Although no single clustering algorithm is optimal for every scenario, the goal remains to identify high-performing methods for specific tasks while filtering out consistently underperforming ones. Evaluating clustering is typically done through either internal validity metrics, such as average compactness or separability, or external indices comparing results to expert ground truths. While internal measures have uncertain validity due to potential meaningfulness of clusters, classical external indices (e.g., normalised mutual information, Fowlkes-Mallows index, and adjusted Rand index), which rely on set-partition similarities, often fall short as well; they struggle to correctly identify pathological cases and can fluctuate depending on the true number of clusters, often lacking interpretability (e.g., the specific implication of an 0.8 score). Consequently, applying the normalised mutual information approach and such measures makes comparative analyses across numerous benchmarks difficult. To address these limitations, this study proposes and analyzes an alternative metric: a chance-corrected, asymmetric optimal set matching accuracy adjusted for cluster imbalance, designed for better performance evaluation consistency.

The study of symmetry within Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ occupies a foundational place in complexity theory, most notably regarding symmetric functions which exhibit invariance under the $S_n$ permutation action. This notion extends to transitive or weakly-symmetric functions; those for which a transitive subgroup $G \subseteq S_n$ leaves the function value invariant when reordering its input bits via an element of $G$. Research into the complexity properties of such transitive functions has been substantial. This work specifically examines these functions through the lens of specific combinatorial measures, aiming to identify the maximum disparity possible between such pairs for the class of transitive functions—a topic thoroughly explored for the broader class of general Boolean functions and recently consolidated by Aaronson et al. in their work from STOC (2021). While significant results in establishing separations between combinatorial pairs often rely on celebrated constructions like Ambainis et al.'s "pointer functions" and Aaronson et al.'s "cheat-sheet functions," most of these established functions fail to be transitive, leaving gaps regarding separations specifically among transitive functions without prior examples. This paper rectifies this by proposing modifications to existing functions and constructing transitive variants capable of revealing comparable separations between these combinatorial pairs of measures.

As classification models increasingly become widespread daily, various tools have emerged for interpreting and evaluating them. Standard methods, such as LIME and SHAP, reveal the importance of input features relative to individual classifier outputs, while numerical metrics like accuracy allow for performance comparisons between models. However, existing literature lacks methods that compare a data feature's impact across multiple distinct classifiers. Such comparative interpretations are vital for uncovering foundational differences between models, selecting an optimal classifier under varying feature constraints, and enhancing model ensembles. To address this, we introduce a Learning-from-Disagreement (LFD) framework designed to visually contrast pairs of classifiers. LFD focuses on data instances yielding divergent predictions from the two models, training a classifier-discriminator specifically using a curated dataset of discrepancies. In the event classifier training features are inaccessible, the discriminator is trained on proposed meta-features—based on theoretical hypotheses regarding classifier behavior—to mimic probing mechanisms post-decision. By leveraging SHAP values on the discriminator's learned meta-features, we provide actionable insights, supplementing our work with metrics that characterize meta-feature importance from various angles. Through visualization of these metrics, identification of complementary discriminator behaviors between the two models occurs. Applying this framework with binary classifiers deployed in banking and advertising, the study evaluates the approach and demonstrates how these tools facilitate more informed integration of classifiers.

This study applies the evolving concept of Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) to Drone Air Vehicle (UAV) networking to minimize age of information (AoI) within communication systems. This design leverages both deep learning for superior feature representation and model-driven physics via the unsupervised loss and a physics-aware network structure. Topologically interlocked architectures are assembled by locking blocks together through geometric constraints enforced by friction and physical contact. When interfacial frictional forces remain intact to the highest possible degree relative to applied stress, blocks remain locked in place yet allow extensive rotational movement before frictional limits are reached. Once these interfacial thresholds are breached relative to frictional strength, sliding occurs at block interfaces, altering the structural mechanical behavior. Enhancing key metrics like strength and toughness has historically remained a primary research focus. Yet, essential questions about how block rotations and interface mechanisms (specifically stick-slip dynamics) influence structures remain largely unexplored. In this study, we execute a parametric analysis to elucidate how block geometry, Young's modulus, and friction coefficient dictate whether a specific system exhibits slip-dominated or stick-governed behavior. By merging analytical methods with computational approaches, we model both mechanical responses and failure modes in beam-style interlocked configurations. This modeling employs a penalty-based finite element technique to manage contact limitations at junctions. Our findings indicate that the ratio of structural height to friction coefficient determines the transition between failure modes controlled by slipping or sticking mechanisms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that rotational motion alongside sustained stopping forces at all contact points create a specific performance ceiling for any given configuration, regardless of its specific material or dimensions. This discovery establishes a definable upper limit for structural responses in these interlocked designs and serves as a foundational performance benchmark from which to evaluate effectiveness and ensure optimal performance.

This study investigates synchrony within a network of Stuart-Landau oscillators utilizing frequency-modulated coupling. Significantly, we identified atypical transition dynamics specific to these amplitudes-characterizing synchronized clusters; specifically, we defined two distinct phases of state evolution: the Bellerophon phase, marked by the formation of alternating phase states in two steps. In its initial stage, chaotic phase synchronization is achieved, followed subsequently by the establishment of a periodical phase synchronization phase, encompassed within a broader regime of Bellerophon states in the system with amplitude dynamics. Our analysis shows that the presence of a regime of Bellerophon states is also achievable in systems of coupled oscillators.

Simulating the mechanical properties of complex, heterogeneous materials is vital for tasks like topology optimization and multi-scale structural analysis. While many WebAssembly (Wasm) programs originate from imperative, memory-insecure languages like C or C++, the translation does not guarantee security; attackers can still exploit vulnerabilities such as use-after frees and buffer overflows within the Wasm environment just as readily as on native systems. The Memory-Safe WebAssembly (MSWasm) approach aims to resolve these threats by extending the runtime with built-in, fine-grained checks tailored at the programming language level. Building upon the conceptual framework originally outlined for MSWasm, this paper formalizes its foundations by establishing precise semantic definitions that demonstrate any well-typed MSWasm program inherently yields to memory-safety checks by design. Central to this development is a new, portable definition of memory-safety rooted in colored pointers and memory regions. This theoretical construct not only underpins safety proofs but also validates the security properties of a C-to-MSWasm compiler, confirming that such a tool generates exclusively safe outputs while accurately reflecting the semantics of already secure programs in safe modes. Leveraging these theoretical guarantees, we implemented several distinct tools, including two transpilers for compiling MSWasm to native machine code and an enhanced Clang-based C-to-MSWasm compiler, which offer varied enforcement mechanisms to balance performance against security based on user requirements. Experimental results indicate that enforcing spatial safety incurs a roughly 22% overhead, whereas full memory safety enforcement results in a higher cost of nearly double (198%). Crucially, the flexible architecture of the MSWasm proposal enables easy switching among enforcement strategies, ensuring the runtime can readily adopt and leverage emerging hardware optimizations and faster execution methods when they mature.

Deep embedding learning aims to construct a metric space where inter-class and intra-class features are distinctly separated, maximizing performance for face recognition (FR) and person re-identification (re-ID). Recent advancements have centered on using discriminative deep embedding to address the open-set problem within these fields. Concurrently, our study identifies data imbalance—a prevalent issue often overlooked in FR and re-ID—as a critical driver of performance decline, yet the mechanisms by which standard softmax or its variants handle (or worsen) this problem remains poorly understood from the angles of optimization and feature distribution. To address this, we theoretically explore the impacts of data imbalance on neural network optimization and softax-based feature dynamics. Key to the observed degradation in performance with unbalanced datasets is that the weights of layers prior to the classifier (specifically the penultimate fully-connected layer) diverge significantly from true class centroids within the feature space. Drawing from these insights, we propose a unified solution: the Imbalance-Robust Softmax (IR-Softmax) framework. Capable of handling both open-set vulnerabilities and data imbalance simultaneously, IR-Softmax works by enforcing weight class-center alignment, thereby generalizing effectively to various discriminative softmax variations (which excel in disentangling open classes). Within IR-Softmax, we explicitly re-structure the popular ArcFace (A-Softmax) and Adaptive Angular Margination (AM-Software) functions based on this principle to neutralize imbalance issues. Empirical evaluations conducted on major face recognition benchmarks (LFW, MegaFace) and re-ID datasets (Market-1501, Duke) demonstrate that IR-Softmax achieves superior results against numerous competing state-of-the-art techniques.

Mechanical frequency combs offer the potential to replicate optical frequency combs on a mechanical platform, though past efforts were constrained by rigid requirements on drive power and frequency along with their limited bandwidth and operational complexity. Research into leveraging quantum effects to accelerate battery charging has been extensive; however, translating these concepts into functional devices requires a critical assessment of how storage stability in quantum battery components holds up against environmental noise. Addressing this challenge, this study formally introduces a set of well-defined performance metrics, specifically work capacitances and maximal asymptotic work/energy ratios. These figures determine the upper limits of energy recovery efficiency within models comprising large arrays of identical, independent quantum battery elements. The analysis proceeds by providing explicit calculations for scenarios where the energy storage systems are subjected to both dephasing and depolarizing noise.

Continual learning focuses on rapidly adapting from sequences of tasks. While experience replay methods currently offer significant advantages in overcoming catastrophic forgetting compared to alternatives, they face a common limitation regarding data imbalances between prior and new tasks, potentially exacerbating forgetting issues; furthermore, resolving the stability-plasticity dilemma in this context remains a critical challenge. This paper introduces the Meta-learning update via Multi-scale Knowledge Distillation and Data Augmentation (MMKDDA) framework, formulated to overcome these hurdles. By leveraging multiscale knowledge distillation to capture the evolution of short- and long-range spatial features across various levels, our approach mitigates the impact of data imbalances. Furthermore, we integrate episodic memory and current-task samples throughout the continuous learning phase, reducing negative influences stemming from probability distribution shifts. In addition, our model utilizes meta-learning optimization weighted by the prior experience distribution to enhance the stability-plasticity trade-off, with experimental validation on four benchmark datasets substantiating the framework's effectiveness over state-of-the-art baselines. Ablation studies further elucidate the specific function of each proposed component.

This analysis searches for Higgs bosons decaying into light pseudoscalar bosons with masses between 4 and 15 GeV, where one decays to a tau-lepton pair and the other to either tau- or muon-lepton pairs. Utilizing proton-proton collision data gathered in 2016 by the CMS experiment at 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, researchers analyzed both $4\tau$ and $2\mu2\tau$ channels. By combining these channels and leveraging the linear relationship between the pseudoscalar's fermionic coupling strength and fermion mass, upper limits on the product of the Higgs production cross-section and its branching ratio ($\sigma\mathcal{B}$) were established relative to the standard model Higgs rate. No significant excess above standard model expectations was detected; consequently, the 95% confidence level observed limits on $\sigma\mathcal{B}$ ranged from 0.022 to 0.23, and the corresponding expected limits from 0.027 to 0.19 within the analyzed mass spectrum.

Tchebycheffian splines represent smooth piecewise functions where each segment arises from (sometimes varying) Tchebycheff spaces, serving as a natural extension of polynomial algebraic spaces. They inherit most standard properties of polynomial splines. Specifically, under appropriate conditions, they can be expressed using TB-splines—a class of basis functions structurally similar to polynomial B-splines. Notably, a compelling subclass includes Tchebycheffian splines composed of null-spaces of constant-coefficient linear differential operators. This allows the integration of polynomials, exponential, and trigonometric functions with unlimited adjustable shape parameters. Furthermore, effective procedures for their calculation and handling are now well-developed. In the following work, TB-splines from this null-space subclass are proposed as a superior alternative to conventional polynomial B-splines and rational NURBS for isogeometric Galerkin methods. We examine leveraging the extensive geometrical and analytical versatility of these Tchebycheff spaces through problem-dependent selection techniques. Consequently, TB-splines provide a broad and resilient framework for isogeometric methodologies that transcends the constraints of the rational NURBS approach.

Although two-dimensional convolutional neural networks (2D-CNNs) often exploit channel statistics for domain manipulation within image processing—rendering instance normalization a successful technique for domain-invariant features—our analysis indicates that domain-relevant cues in audio features are anchored primarily in frequency statistics rather than channel data. Driven by this observation, we propose Relaxed Instance Frequency-wise Normalization (RFN), an explicit plug-and-play module that regularizes elements along the frequency dimension. This module effectively removes instance-level domain discrepancies in acoustic features while mitigating the loss of critical discriminative information. Empirical results from acoustic scene classification tasks demonstrate significant performance over prior domain generalization methods and enhance robustness across varied audio input devices. Notably, RFN secured first place in the DCASE2021 TASK1A challenge for low-complexity acoustic scene classification across multiple devices with clear winners margins, building upon the technical report released previously.

Achieving automatic garment manipulation is particularly difficult because of the enormous variance in how these items deform. To mitigate this inherent uncertainty, we introduce "canonicalized-alignment," a technique that reduces the feasible space of garment states to facilitate subsequent tasks. We conceptualize this as a "cloth-state funnel," which deforms arbitrary clothing into a fixed, predefined pose comprising exact rigid orientation (alignment) and a simplified deformation pattern (canonicalization). Converting garments into a compact collection of highly visible, structured shapes creates ideal conditions for manipulation operations. To overcome learning challenges such as adverse local minima, we define a specialized optimization function. Leveraging this goal, we train a robust, general-purpose robotic policy utilizing multiple manipulator arms; this policy seamlessly selects between dynamic throwing maneuvers and slower, quasi-static grasping techniques to effectively canonicalize fabric items. We validate our framework on a physical ironing and folding rig, employing this learned approach as a foundational layer. Our empirical analysis confirms that a paradigm which is agnostic to specific tasks can boost the efficacy of even hand-coded policies in scenarios where previous automation failed, effectively unifying rigid, deformable-manufacturing automation, and accessible code with visual results. Physics-derived forecasts of solar cycles offer a potent method to validate current models. Numerous theoretical predictions leveraging Flux Transport (FTD) or Surface Flux Transport (SFT) models—and some combining both—were established prior to Cycle 25. The underlying mechanism shared by these forecasts relies on the notion that poloidal magnetic fields near cycle minimum dictate the future cycle's peak. This overview begins by briefly explaining FVT and SFT frameworks. Next, it contrasts seven such predictor models across four criteria: the variable used as the predictor, the methodology to derive it, the approach for implementation, and the specific target values forecasted. Additionally, the study highlights through SFT numerical experiments the substantial impact assimilated magnetograms have on prediction outcomes. The paper further advocates for incorporating uncertainties in both initial surface magnetograms and sunspot emergence into physics-led forecasting due to their pronounced influence. Lastly, the review focuses primarily on insights to be garnered from diverse predictions instead of strictly evaluating which prediction results were accurate or incorrect.

Whereas numerous prior investigations resolve dynamics in the Einstein frame using a conventional Einstein-Hilbert action, we introduce a methodology to solve equations of motion within the native Jordan frame, where explicit non-minimal couplings are retained. This algorithm accommodates minimally coupled sectors alongside any number of scalars with non-minimal interactions, accounting for cosmic expansion driven by all participating fields. The framework is applicable to complex scenarios featuring full inhomogeneity, highly non-linear dynamics arising from effects like mode-rescattering and backreaction, and regimes where the universe expands due to non-minimal fields entirely. To illustrate, we explore geometric preheating triggered by a spectator non-minimally coupled scalar while an inflaton oscillates post-inflation. Ultimately, this technique may provide new insights into the quantum mechanical equivalence between the Jordan and Einstein formulations.

Due to the inherent design of mobile systems, credential leakage through shoulder surfing—an observation-based attack—is a primary threat during the device unlocking process. Potential Peccei-Quinn (PQ) symmetries are susceptible to various forms of explicit breaking, which are well-known for potentially disrupting axion solutions to the strong CP problem and, under specific conditions, generating anomalously large axion masses. Two predominant corrections to standard calculations involving such breaking are higher-dimension symmetry-breaking operators—in scenarios where a complex field triggers spontaneous PQ breaking—and small instantons. Inspired by contexts where small instantons dominate the $\theta}$ potential of non-abelian gauge theories, we frame axion quality concerns through the lens of constraints on a Wilsonian effective action at energy scales just above those of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). Within this framework, the conventional axion mass derivation relies on an almost exact PQ symmetry. Consequently, higher-dimension terms or small instantons act as symmetry-breaking contributions within the Wilsonian action. This unified perspective addresses axion quality by showing that if high-energy CP violation occurs naturally (with order-one coupling), satisfying constraints for the strong CP problem requires these terms in the action to keep the axion mass extraordinarily proximate to its "standard" value.

Driven by insights from the early-time dynamics of quark-gluon plasmas formed in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, we utilize linear response theory combined with classical-statistical lattice simulations to derive gluonic spectral functions from overfilled gauge theories operating far from equilibrium. Our analysis of a $2+1$-dimensional spacetime reveals that while the spectral function displays quasiparticle-like excitations at all momenta in $3+1$ dimensions—results largely aligning with perturbative hard-thermal loop predictions despite some nonperturbative deviations—it exhibits markedly different, intrinsically nonpertur\-bative excitation structures in $2+1$ dimensions. These unavoidable strong interactions result in broad peaks within the spectral function, confirming the lack of soft quasiparticles in such theories. Consequently, nonperten\-bative effects likely provide significant corrections to systems featuring strong momentum anisotropy, which is crucial for correctly interpreting phenomenological results from heavy-ion collision research.

Automatically locating the specific code changes that introduce software bugs offers the potential to boost both developer productivity and the overall quality of software systems. Evaluation metrics indicate the proposed model offers marked improvements, demonstrating significant advantages over baselines.

Handling missing data presents a significant challenge in machine learning. Guided by the premise that imputation strategies ought to safeguard the data's causal structure, we propose a regularization framework designed to force standard imputation techniques to align causalistically with their data generation processes. Our method, known as MIRACLE (Causally-aware Imputation), functions by iteratively upgrading initial imputations; it does so while concurrently modeling the mechanism causing missingness to ensure consistency with causal structures. Through rigorous testing on both synthetic and numerous real datasets, we demonstrate that MIRACLE consistently surpasses various benchmark approaches across all major missingness patterns: completely missing at random (MCAR), at random (MAR), and missing not at random (MNAR).

This paper extends methodology within the Differences in Differences (DiD) literature by demonstrating that both additive and multiplicative Standard Structural Nested Mean Models (SNMM), along with coarse variants (Robins, 1994-2004; Lok and Degruttola, 2012; Vansteelandt and Joffe, 2014), remain identified under parallel trends assumptions. The approach facilitates adjustments for dynamic covariates, characterizes effect heterogeneity based on these variables, estimates various causal contrasts—such as transient ("blip" effects) and controlled direct effects—and accommodates a wide spectrum of treatment patterns. Notably, these extensions incur no stronger requirements for validity, as they adhere only to parallel trends conditions comparable to those standard in DiD research, while also including a method for sensitivity testing against assumption violations. Unlike much of the existing DiD work, however, our focus is strictly on panel data rather repeated cross-sectional datasets. Furthermore, we outline an approach to derive optimal treatment regimes using optimal regieme SNMM under parallel trends alongside an extra, stringent assumption of no confounder-induced effect modification. The study culminates in real-world applications assessing the impact of bank deregulation on real estate values and how floods influence flood insurance enrollment rates.

With the expansion of Natural Language Processing (NLP) into sensitive domains such as political profiling and educational assessment review, there is a pressing need to enhance NLP model transparency to foster stakeholder trust and uncover biases. Self-organized criticality (SOC) has been suggested as a universal mechanism driving the occurrence of scale-free dynamics across diverse complex systems and possibly within the brain. Although experimental studies have confirmed these scale-free patterns in various neural recordings, the biological mechanisms underpinning them were previously elusive. Building on these findings, synaptic plasticity was proposed in network models capable of self-organizing neuronal activity toward a critical point. This survey examines how methods enforcing multiple timescales and grounded in biological plausibility were utilized within these models to regulate the number and potency of neural connections, thereby shifting dynamic states. Certain plasticity rules promote stability near criticality, whereas others risk driving the system away from this state unless accompanied by supplementary stabilizing mechanisms. We introduce a classification framework based on the duration that near-critical dynamics persist after a rule's inactivation. Additionally, we consider the implications of self-organized criticality for neural computation, concluding that while aiding these concepts clarifies brain function, living neuronal networks appear to exploit not only critical regimes but also the deviations surrounding them for their overall operations.

Video grounding focuses on identifying the specific time intervals in an unedited video clip that match a given textual description. Most current methods utilize two main frameworks: either a Top-down approach that pre-defines candidate segments for classification and boundary refinement, or a Bottom-up approach that predicts boundary probabilities on a frame-by-frame basis. Nonetheless, existing models are not entirely end-to-end, as they depend on computationally intensive post-processing to polish results. To address this, we recast video grounding as a set prediction problem and introduce GTR, a new multi-modal Transformer architecture. GRT comprises dedicated video and language encoders alongside a cross-modal decoder for the grounding task. To enable efficient end-to-end training, we employ a Cubic Embedding layer converting raw input into visual tokens, while a designed Multi-head Cross-Modal Attention module enhances modal integration within the decoder. The model is optimized using a Many-to-One matching loss. Additionally, extensive analyses were conducted to test various design configurations. Evaluations across three benchmarks demonstrate GTR's superiority; its typical variants set new performance records on all datasets and metrics while achieving inference speeds multiple times faster than existing methods.

This study addresses a broad class of online stochastic optimization tasks characterized by multiple concurrent budget constraints over a finite time interval. During each period, both a reward and a set of costs, which correspond individually to budget expenditures, are observed after the decision-maker selects an action from a convex, compact set; selected budgets accumulate. Unlike previous assumptions, both these reward and cost structures emerge randomly from time-varying, unknown distributions. The primary objective involves maximizing the total accrued reward while respecting all budget limitations. While this model is versatile enough to represent applications such as online linear programming and network revenue management, it is further divided into two distinct frameworks: first, a data-driven scenario where a potentially imprecise prior estimate of the true distribution exists, secondly an uninformative setting where this true distribution remains almost entirely unknown without a prior estimate. We introduce an adaptive Wasserstein-distance based metric designed to quantify both potential errors in prior assumptions for setting (i) and inherent system non-stationarity for setting (ii). Our analysis establishes that this specific measure provides both necessary and sufficient criteria for achieving sublinear regret across both frameworks. For setting (i), we develop an enhanced algorithm employing primal-dual principles to integrate information from the underlying distributions directly into the dual-space variant of an online stochastic gradient descent (OSGD). Furthermore, with appropriate adaptation, this approach naturally aligns with setting (ii). Regardless of which setting applies, both proposed algorithms achieve the theoretically optimal order of regret. Finally, numerical results illustrate the effectiveness of combining our algorithms with techniques for dynamic scheme resolution to significantly enhance their operational performance.

Stellar variability acts as a primary barrier to achieving the sensitivity needed for Radial Velocity (RV) methods to detect Earth-like exoplanets. The study addresses the question of what data prerequisites are necessary to engineer a potent outlier/out-of-distribution (OOD) discriminator, specifically targeting inputs that deviate significantly from the training data. While unlabeled in-distribution (IID) samples are abundant in many contexts and should form the basis for ideal detectors, we note that most existing models relying solely on unlabled data perform poorly, often matching the rate or random guessing. Meanwhile, current state-of-the-art OOD solutions require access to fine-grained class labels for supervised training to deliver superior results. We introduce SSD, a novel outlier detection method trained exclusively on unlabeled in-distribution samples by combining self-supervised representation learning with Mahalanobis distance measurement in the feature space. Empirical results indicate SSD outperforms most existing unlabeled-based detectors substantially, and can match, or occasionally exceed, the performance of supervised detectors. Beyond the baseline, we develop two key extensions to the framework: first, a version supporting few-shot OOD detection with access to only 1–5 labeled samples per outlier class, and second, an adaptation that leverages training data labels when available. These extensions enhance SSD's performance, ultimately achieving the highest ranking among detected methods. Our source code is publicly hosted at https://github.com/inspire-group/SSD.

We introduce a generalized version of this method that ensures adaptability to avoid bias while accessing an exponentially large set of energy-equal configurations. We assess its versatility within both Markov chain Monte-Carlo frameworks and genetic algorithms, demonstrating efficacy through Ising model sampling across diverse graph types and resolution of established binary optimization challenges. Our findings hold significance both theoretically and practically for research in spin glasses, with wider implications for the field of discrete optimization since countless issues mirror Ising spin system structures.

We introduce TXPipe, a modular, automated, and highly reproducible workflow designed to create data vectors for cosmological analysis within the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC). Focused specifically on the $3\times 2\mathrm{pt}$ analysis—a method combining three two-point functions to measure auto- and cross-correlations between galaxy density and shapes—the pipeline processes data in both real and harmonic spaces alongside other LSST-DESC tools. Validations through Gaussian simulations demonstrate that TXPipe measures data vectors precisely and reconstructs the input cosmology, meeting the accuracy standards expected for the inaugural year of LSST observations. Additionally, we applied TXPipe to a realistic mock galaxy set drawn from the CosmoDC2 simulation suite (Korytov et al. 2019). By establishing this foundational framework, TXPipe serves as a scalable baseline for the ongoing LSST survey and is readily extendable to address future scientific investigations beyond the $3\times 2\mathrm{pt}$ analysis.

As a real-time operating system (RTOS) with configurable scheduling options, FreeRTOS stands as one of the most favored solutions for embedded devices, attributed to its high level of portability and customizability. We develop a formal model for the FreeRTOS ARM Cortex-M4 port and use model checking to detect errors in the models associated with example FreeRTOS applications. Surprisingly, faults were identified in our application models under various scheduling policies. To verify these findings, we updated programs released free to distribution, reconfirming assertion failures on the STM32F429I-DISC board.

By applying the timing argument in conjunction with current observations and standard cosmological initial conditions, we have identified consistent orbital paths for MW-M31. Modeling both galaxies as point masses and integrating the paths of test-particle disks nearby allows us to delineate tidal remnants.

Our simulations reveal that tidal debris clusters near specific orbital poles for each galaxy. In several models, these theoretical spin axes align well with the observed orientations of the satellites' planes, and the material's radial distribution matches reality. Regarding the Milky Way, our preferred model suggests a 24% component of counter-rotating material within the thick disk, which may account for Sculptor's reverse rotation. However, our results show no such counter-rotating material around M31, a finding verifiable via future proper motion data. OpenMP has become the standard API for parallel programming in high-performance computing applications. Because such programs often reside in data centers—where energy efficiency is paramount—we analyze various aspects of OpenMP from an energy perspective, contrasting with previous work focused primarily on performance. Our methodology involves measuring energy usage across data center nodes via novel microbenchmarks and established benchmark suites. We examine three specific areas of behavior: loop tiling and auto-unrolling, comparisons between `parallel-for` loops and explicit tasks, and thread management policies involving spinning versus blocked threading. Regarding loops, our tests indicate that for certain non-optimized programs, loop tiling can deliver significant energy reductions, while auto-unrolling offers minimal improvement at best and degrades performance in severe scenarios. In comparisons of loop styles, both approaches are applicable in specific cases, "parallel-for" frequently outperforms explicit tasks an effect which grows as the workload becomes finer-grained. Regarding thread management, allowing non-scheduled threads to spin occasionally saves energy more effectively than descheduling, despite increasing individual power consumption for those instances. Additionally, we assess compiler influence (testing with Intel ICC, Clang, and GCC variants). While no single compiler is consistently superior, they can yield markedly different outcomes for identical code. Finally, by synthesizing all these findings, we recommend novel compiler directives and general guidelines aimed at optimizing the energy efficiency of OpenMP applications.

Model learning, alternatively known as active automata learning, serves as a powerful method for deriving black-box finite state models from software systems. Specifically, we present updated versions of RALib's Tree and Equivalence oracles that leverage these derived constraints. Using a tainting tool adapted for Python, we generate constraints from code execution histories and pit this grey-box variant of RALib against the established black-box original across multiple benchmarks, including various data structures within the Python standard library. Our proof-of-concept demonstrates an efficacy boost of nearly two orders of magnitude regarding the quantity of inputs transmitted to the target software. Notably, this approach, applicable to broader model categories, empowers RALib to learn models beyond the capability of pure black-box techniques, such as those involved in combination lock systems.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) represent a groundbreaking communication technology capable of controlling the wireless channel through cost-efficient, intelligently managed reflective panels. Yet, relying solely on passive reflection to surpass traditional systems demands an excessively large surface area. Addressing this limitation, recent research introduced the active RIS, which not only reflects signals but also amplifies them at the added expense of power usage to overcome performance bottlenecks. Building on this, this paper presents a new beamforming methodology termed "over-the-air" beamforming, designed for RIS-facilitated multi-user multiple-input single-output (MISO) systems. A key feature of our design is eliminating the need for complex pre-/post-signal processing at the transmitters and receivers. By tailoring individual RIS active reflection coefficients to optimize sum-rate gains, our proposed approach tackles transmission efficiency. The solution addresses this as a challenging non-convex, quadratically constrained quadratic program. We resolve this by applying the semidefinite relaxation (SDR) technique, which transforms the problem into a convex feasibility task efficiently solvable via CVX. Furthermore, deriving inspiration from these insights, we devise an innovative, high-throughput receive index modulation scheme equipped with a computationally efficient, suboptimal detector. Simulations thoroughly demonstrate the proposed systems, analyzing both sum-rate capacity and bit error rate (BER) performance improvements.

As agents cross community boundaries, this process allows influence to disseminate, occasionally resulting in the rise of a shared signal across groups. Neutrinos experience rapid flavor oscillations known as fast flavor instabilities (FFI) within the dense cores of collapsing supernovae and during neutron star mergers. Consequently, significant flavor transformation can dramatically influence both supernova explosion mechanisms and the subsequent enrichment of the universe with heavy elements. Since current state-of-the-art simulations of supernovae and mergers often use moment-based algorithms for neutrino transport rather than angular information, it has been difficult to conclusively determine where these systems are unstable to FFI. This study evaluates various existing moment-based diagnostic criteria by conducting stationary, general relativistic neutrino transport simulations based on a snapshot from a 3D neutron star merger, thereby generating testable neutrino distributions for each criterion. Additionally, the authors introduce a novel ``maximum entropy'' test for identifying instabilities; although somewhat more sophisticated, it provides more precise approximations regarding the depth and width of electron lepton number (ELN) crossings than previous methods. The findings indicate that the proposed maximum entropy test and a resonant trajectory analysis prove particularly successful at predicting instability in the simulated snapshot, while all examined tests identify regions where significant flavor transformation is most probable.

This research employed non-equilibrium molecular dynamics to examine the Soret effect within binary mixtures of dimer and monomer systems, specifically isolating how flexible molecules' internal degrees of freedom influence thermal separation. The findings reveal that as the molecules soften, the thermal diffusivity (thermal diffusion) factor declines and potentially inverts its sign, a trend we linked to two proposed mechanisms. This work presents the inaugural observation of $Z$ boson generation in proton-lead collisions performed at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5~\text{TeV}$. A $1.6~\text{nb}^{-1}$ integrated luminosity sample was gathered using the LHCb detector, with $Z$ candidates identified as opposite-sign muon pairs having a transverse momentum exceeding $20~\text{GeV}/c$ within $2.0 \le \text{pseudorapity} \le 4.5$, and an invariant mass constrained between $60$ and $120~\text{GeV}/c^2$. The measured $Z \to \mu^+\mu^-$ cross-section is $\sigma(\text{fwd})=13.5^{+5.4}_{-4.0}\text{(stat.)}\pm1.2\text{(syst.)}~\text{nb}$ along the proton beam direction, and $\sigma(\text{bwd}) = 10.7^{+8.4}_{-5.1}\text{(stat.)}\pm1.0\text{(syst.)}~\text{nb}$ along the lead beam direction. In this study, we evaluate how image magnification affects the Dark Energy Survey's Year 3 analysis, specifically focusing on galaxy clustering and galaxy-galaxy lensing. Our investigation employs two distinct lens populations: Luminous red galaxies identified via the redMaGiC catalog and redshift-dependent selection limits defined in the MagLim sample. Utilizing Balrog simulations to handle systematic uncertainties, we quantify the distortion in both galaxy flux and size selection, finding a notable bias in the MagLim sample if magnification is ignored. While allowing for magnification biases by $\Lambda$CDM or wcdE cosmologies yields parameters broadly consistent across various magnification prior assumptions, freeing the magnitude bias amplitude reveals a tension: observed two-point correlations favor values that diverge from those predicted by simulation-based fiducial inputs. Furthermore, cross-clustering measurements within lens redshift bins contrast the magnitude bias with the cross-clustering between bins predicted using only intra-bin luminaires, with these deviations pointing to non-kinetic systematics beyond magnification as possible culprits. Our approach improves by including the cross-clustering, significantly tightening lens magnification constraints while permitting non-kinetic prior volumes without reducing analytical sensitivity.

Face Anti-Spoofing (FAS), an indispensable and prevalent module within recognition architectures, struggles for perpetual perfection. Despite reaching considerable precision levels, real-world factors such as shifting environmental conditions and the emergence of novel presentation attack methods can degrade FAS performance across deployment contexts, hindering universal robustness due to data homogeneity across diverse scenarios. Practically, when abundant labeled face images exist in an initial source domain but only scarce examples from the new FAS domain are provided for a particular target domain, the system is expected to maintain high efficacy for novel unseen attack methods. This study tackles this specific scenario, termed Few-Shot Domain Expansion (FSDE)-based Face Anti-Spoofing (FAS), and proposes that both the new FAS scenarios should be handled accurately without degrading the initial target domain's performance to a critical extent. Segmentation of Complete Renal Structures (3D CRS) aims to simultaneously isolate kidneys, tumors, and associated arteries and veins within a single inference, ultimately offering critical preoperative planning and intraoperative guidance for minimally invasive partial nephrectomy (LPN) to combat kidney cancer. This study addresses these gaps for the first time by employing adversarial ensemble learning to develop Ensemble Multi-condition GAN (EnMcGAN). The research presents three key innovations: first, a "multi-windowing committee," which is inspired by CNN windowing techniques, partitions CTA images into multiple narrow windows with varied settings to sharpen contrasts in soft tissues and organ edges; this feeds into an ensemble model that aggregates segmentation strengths for improved global quality. Second, a "multi-condition GAN" introduced to force the segmented outputs adhere strictly to realistic shape constraints, thereby enhancing feature extraction capabilities related to form. Third, an "adversarial weighted ensemble module," which utilizes trained discriminators to assess segment accuracy per input and normalizes these scores to refine the weighting of the overall ensemble output. In statistical physics, equilibrium states are typically derived from Boltzmann-Gibbs measure averages via ergodic sampling methods like the Langevin dynamics. However, certain quantities, especially transport coefficients— which link a physical force to its resulting current, as exemplified by thermal conductivity where forcing creates energy flow with resistance proportional to conductivity—are beyond the reach of straightforward equilibrium sampling. Conceptually, transport coefficients represent a form of sensitivity regarding imposed forces added to baseline dynamics. Various numerical strategies exist to estimate these coefficients but generally incur large statistical errors. This article examines popular methodologies, including the Green-Kubo relation which defines coefficients through time-integrated correlations of equilibrium data, and perturbation-based techniques relying on the long-time average of stochastically driven (nonequilibrium molecular dynamics) states. Both approaches are analyzed regarding their error structures, detailing specific biases introduced by time discretization and the variance of Monte Carlo estimators. Additionally, emerging alternative numerical techniques for estimating such transport parameters are briefly considered.

This study examines how intrinsic noise impacts the stable states of a one-dimensional dynamical system featuring saddle-node bifurcations between monostability and bistability in its deterministic form. The model, a modified Schlöogl equation for a single-molecule chemical reaction, incorporates variability into intrinsic noise by introducing bursts during the autocatalytic production phase while preserving the underlying deterministic dynamics. Results indicate that adjusting burst magnitude can eliminate or induce these bifurcations, demonstrating that bursty molecule production can qualitatively alter the system's dynamics even when the average behavior remains fixed.

Subspace clustering techniques are essential for revealing cluster structures within datasets, widely employed for exploration across various natural science fields. However, many existing approaches fail to manage unwanted dataset biases. On data containing multiple samples representing diverse attributes, applying standard clustering naively can lead to suboptimal outcomes. To address this limitation, we introduce a new framework designed to jointly remove undesired biases while learning to cluster data points in individual subspaces. Leveraging available bias information, we enhance traditional clustering by adversarially training it to reduce the mutual information between data points and these unwanted attributes. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our methodology.

We introduce a method to induce dynamic distinct superpositions of eigenstates in 2D trapped two-component Bose-Fermi gases via a sudden quench of scattering lengths from an initial non-interacting configuration with adjustable spatial size. When the initial localization width exceeds the three-body harmonic length, the system predominantly evolves into trapped states, where Tan contacts reveal growing short-range two-body and three-body correlations; however, if the initial width lies beneath this threshold, a superposition of trimer and atom-dimer components forms. Increasing the initial extent diminishes the magnitude of such many-body effects, yet distinct peaks remain at energy spectrum avoided crossing points, marking the influence of atom-dimers. These findings demonstrate controlled excitation schemes to selectively generate triply and dimer-correlated bound states as well as confined few-body levels, phenomena potentially observable with existing laboratory setups capable of precise parameter control.

Despite the study of single-molecule protein folding dynamics using Single-Molecule Force Spectroscopy (SMFS) over the past two decades, a universally standardized approach for data analysis and communal sharing remains missing. To address this, we introduce Fodis, a new open-source software designed to analyze Force-Distance curves from SMFS. This toolkit offers near-automatic data preprocessing, analysis, and classification, enabling users to distinguish various protein unfolding trajectories as well as identify structural heterogeneities occurring throughout the unfolding process.

Human motion prediction focuses on anticipating several distinct future sequences from observed pose data. Prior methods typically use deep generative networks to model the conditional data distribution followed by random sampling; although these methods produce varying outcomes, they generally converge to the most probable results, which lacks necessary diversity. Lately, research has moved toward deterministically learning various modes of this distribution using specific networks, yet such approaches remain limited by the number of fixed modes and their specific ranges. In our work, we introduce a new sampling strategy capable of extracting high variance results from unbalanced multi-modal distributions trained by deep generative models. Our approach functions by constructing an auxiliary space where random sampling within that space equates to retrieving diverse samples from the target distribution. We present an uncomplicated yet powerful neural architecture adopting this strategy, utilizing Gumbel-softmax matrix sampling and a divergence-focused hinge loss function. Substantial experiments show this method markedly boosts both diversity and precision compared to existing best-in-class sampling techniques, and our code along with pre-trained models can be found at https://github.com/Droliven/diverse_sampling.

In response, we develop a unique system identification method capable of learning effectively even from failed attempts. We validated a solution upon a ROBOTIS-OP3 humanoid using these techniques, resulting in the deployment of a transferred control policy capable of stabilizing and walking the robot on uneven terrain while withstanding severe perturbations—achieved entirely without relying on external force and torque sensors.

Based on this finding, a novel technique known as Robust Soft Label Adversarial Distillation (RSLAD) was developed specifically for training resilient lightweight models. RSLAD comprehensively leverages robust soft labels from a large, adversarially augmented teacher to optimize the learning of small student models using both clean and attacked data across all objective functions. Empirical results show that RSLAD significantly outperforms existing training and distillation strategies in terms of robustness when defending small models against leading attacks such as AutoAttack. Furthermore, the discussion offers insights into the proposed RSLAD methodology and underscores the critical role of robust soft labels within adversarial robustness.

News serves as a relevant but difficult resource for assessing financial stress and risks because natural language is unstructured and scarce. We propose using distributional semantics and deep neural network learning to connect news text with a limited collection of documented bank failure occurrences. By employing unsupervised training, we derive semantic vector representations of news stories to serve as foreicators of distressed bank events. Our learning algorithm generates signals of co-occurring stress at both the individual bank and the aggregate European level, while enabling the immediate retrieval of text descriptions highlighting specific distressed episodes based on their stress levels. Notably, our method yields unique insights compared to those based on alternative data sources and provides an explainable framework to interpret this form of semantic prediction. Grounding this approach, we model bank insolvency using a dataset of 6.6 million news stories and 243 distress events covering 101 major European financial institutions.

Furthermore, we assessed constraints regarding both the ULIRG population's contribution to diffuse astrophysical neutrino detections and various theoretical models.

Although gene expression-based cancer classification facilitates early diagnosis and recovery, it is significantly challenged by the presence of a vast number of genes relative to the sample size. These selected features undergo Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to adjust gene count requirements for quantum bits. Subsequent steps involve using the selected reduced-dataset to guide a quantum simulator in estimating kernels for an initial quantum kernel matrix generation, with classical computing utilized thereafter to determine support vectors based on this matrix alongside the predictive phase. The proposed method was applied to colon and breast microarray datasets—simultaneously utilizing all and BAHO-selected genes—demonstrably improving overall performance with both sets. Furthermore, the approach's validity was assessed by testing various quantum feature maps to create specific kernels compared to the classic Radial Basis Function (RBF).

This research explores the chaotic trajectories of a heavy body navigating perturbed Schwarzschild or Kerr spacetimes. We identify three new orbit types unique to these perturbed scenarios. Second, we reveal orbits that oscillate between a confined area and infinity, drawing a parallel to solutions in the Newtonian three-body problem. Third, our findings indicate that in the perturbed Kerr geometry, certain trajectories swirl near the event horizon before possessing enough escape to leave it entirely.

Research on higher-order topological phases as an extension of the Berry phenomenon is extensive. However, existing theoretical frameworks fail to clarify how connecting lower and higher-order phases extends the relationship from one lattice to another. This work proposes and validates experimentally, through the generation of a topological corner state formed from one-dimensional lattice edges. By implementing spatial modulation of couplings independently for both directions in a 2D square lattice and combining the resulting edge states, we identify the corresponding higher-order corner phase in two dimensions, explicitly revealing dimensional topological connections in this context. Furthermore, considering two modulation phases as synthetic dimensions (as seen in a Aubry--Andre--Harper model instance), these 2D corner states can also be interpreted as a dimensional reduction from a 4D topological phase defined by a vector Chern number. Ultimately, this work advances the comprehension of topological phases across lattice dimensions and offers a promising approach for constructing high-order topo phases in complex structures.

While visual attention maps have been a widely adopted method for illuminating how Visual Question Answer (VQA) models reason by highlighting relevant image or text regions, they can mislead human observers by emphasizing correctly focused areas that the model actually processes inaccurately, resulting in wrong answers. To resolve this discrepancy and enhance clarity, we present Error Maps. This approach specifically highlights the visual regions responsible for a model's inaccuracies, including cases where focused attention does not yield the correct inference, thereby improving user comprehension of error scenarios. To rigorously validate these new explanations, we develop a novel metric designed to simulate and quantify how helpful these interpretations are in ascertaining model correctness. Furthermore, user study results reveal that our Error Maps outperform existing baseline methods, increasing understanding capability of model reliability by 30\%, while our proxy metric exhibits a very high correlation ($\\rho > 0.97$) with users' predicted assessment of correctness.

Convolutional Neural Networks are currently the standard solution for image classification; however, these models do not naturally possess translation invariance. This shortcoming is largely attributed to stride usage, which bypasses the sampling theorem, and the absence of spatial reasoning within fully connected layers. The authors demonstrate that striding significantly enhances translation invariance when accompanied by local homogeneity—sufficuent similarity between adjacent pixels—and note that the presence of this characteristic varies by dataset and dictates the specific pooling kernel size and stride configuration needed for invariance. Furthermore, the study identifies a critical trade-off regarding pooling kernel size: while larger kernels promote higher translation invariance, they compromise model generalization. Lastly, the authors examine other established techniques, including global average pooling, anti-aliased operations, and data augmentation, evaluating their efficacy both empirically and relative to the concept of local homogeneity.

Emerging interest has focused on medical report generation to produce lengthy, coherent textual descriptions corresponding to given medical images. Comprehending the ambient environment is critical for various tasks, including autonomy in navigation and vehicle operations. However, capturing real-world imaging data with precise per-pixel annotations presents significant challenges. Currently, existing synthetic datasets offer high accuracy yet remain restricted primarily to indoors under static lighting and fixed scene conditions, thus severely constraining their utility for outdoor applications. This study presents OmniHorizon, a novel synthetic resource containing 24,335 omnidirectional images covering a wide spectrum of both interior and exterior environments—spanning architecture, roadways, and varied foliage. The dataset simulates dynamic elements such as changing illumination, time of day variables, and moving objects like people and cars. Additionally, the paper introduces a demonstrated cross-domain synthetic-to-real inference technique specifically for estimating 3D scene depth and surface normals in open-world scenarios using this dataset. To achieve this, a newly proposed architecture named UBotNet—derived from a UNet combined with Bottleneck Transformer blocks—is employed to generate faithful normal estimates relative to the scene's geometry. Experimental results indicate that UBotNet yields substantial performance gains, delivering a 4.6% boost in depth accuracy and a 5.75% improvement in normal estimation relative to other networks such as skip-connection U-Nets. The authors further validate these findings by demonstrating the effectiveness of UBotNet in processing real-world imagery using solely images derived from the OmniHorizon training set, highlighting the potential of both their dataset approach and network structure for advanced scene understanding.

A topological pump facilitates the robust transport of quantized particles by cyclically varying system parameters. This finding establishes a pathway for investigating topological pumping in disordered topological crystals while delivering adaptable platforms for stable transport mechanisms.

The growing sophistication of systems-on-a-chips (SoCs) necessitates the ongoing advancement of electronics design automation tools, with virtual platform simulation becoming a widespread practice for SoCs. These virtual platforms enhance hardware/software co-design, accelerate time-to-market, and facilitate model analysis and debugging; consequently, profiling tools are essential to boost their utility. Such tools collect simulated data during runs for post-hoc evaluation to uncover details about both the simulation and the underlying executed software. This work introduces NISTT, a tracing instrument capable of profiling SystemC-TLM-2.0 based virtual platforms. Unlike other approaches, NISTT operates completely non-intrusively, meaning it functions without modifying the simulation process or needing access to its source code, and it operates regardless of the simulation run's presence of debug symbols. Standard SystemC application programming interfaces assure NISTT's flexibility across different simulation environments. A case study illustrates the tool's effectiveness: NISTT was attached to a virtual platform to trace the Linux boot process. Post-simulation, the generated database was assessed, and the outputs were visualized. Finally, an evaluation of the profiling overhead revealed that NISTT exerts minimal impact on overall simulation performance.

This paper marks a significant advancement in neural network explainability by framing explanations as answers to abstract, reasoning-focused queries. For a model prediction $P$ given a contrast option $Q$, the core inquiries include ``Why P?'', ``What if not P?'', and ``Why P, yet not Q?' '. Correspondingly, their answers—derived observationally—correspond to correlations, counterfactuals, and contrastive explanations. Collectively, these form an abductive reasoning framework which we designate the observed explanatory paradigms. The qualifier "observed" specifically addresses the post-hoc nature of these models, where techniques interpret an already-drawn decision. A distinct benefit of this abductive perspective is that explanations serve as valid justifications within future decisions, transforming the post-hoc field merely a justification tool into an active component in decision-making. By offering specific but contextually rich interventions during the process, this approach enhances the relevance of post-facto analysis. The paper's key contributions comprise: ($i$) conceptualizing explanations through the lens of reasoning paradigms; ($ii$) establishing a probabilistic definition alongside criteria for the completeness of these explanations; ($iii$) developing a new evaluation taxonomy for them; ($iv$) situating gradient-based complete explainability to assess replicability and reproducibility across varied tasks and modalities; ($v$) releasing public code repositories available on GitHub.

Beyond this classification system and experimentation, these techniques also allow for an adaptive training strategy that crafts fresh input mixes centered on class pairs most frequently confused by the learner, thus demanding higher nuance to differentiate them. Empirical evaluations across six benchmark datasets confirm that utilizing these diverse input space-expanding transformations is highly effective for generalization, spotting defective samples, and bolstering robustness against attacks.

Training models for 3D lidar-based object detection and semantic segmentation necessitates costly labeling efforts. This newly designed framework utilizes existing scans by intelligently identifying optimal positions to place virtual objects while addressing occlusions directly and maintaining real physical lidar attributes like intensity and ray-drop for inserted scans. This paper addresses information leakage to a guessing adversary within the zero-error source coding framework, governed by a confusion graph that symbolizes distinguishability among source symbols. Leakage quantification relies on measuring the ratio of an adversary's maximal guessing success probability prior to and after eavesdropping the codeword, determined under distributions generated after optimization by the adversary, akin to the maximal leakage metric or worst-case min-measure. This work demonstrates that a Grand Canonical Ensemble (GCE) methodology can effectively determine the phase behavior and structural characteristics of an adhesive substrate subject to self-avoiding polymer strands under terminal pulling forces. By establishing analytic formulations for the mean lengths of fundamental absorbed components like loops and strands via the interaction potential and detach-force, we have calculated the universal exponents influencing their probability densities. This study explores an integrated system combining visible light positioning and communication (VPCCL) utilizing a solitary LED-lamp. This paper examines the algebraic characteristics of binary relations with a "smooth" underlying digraph—a graph containing neither sources nor sinks. These relations are recognized as surjective hyper-operations (shops) on their vertex sets as well as binary mappings defined globally where the inverse is also globally defined; the latter are termed multipermutations. We analyze the lattice structure comprising the (mono)ids of multipermutations acting over an n-element domain. Via a Galois connection, these monoids serve as mathematical analogues for sets of relations closed under definability in positive first-order logic without equality, while our work focuses explicitly on the side involving relation-definability, contrasting it with the previously detailed inverse side. Additionally, we explore the properties of taking inverses for multipermutations and how these link the associated monoids to groups. Utilizing these findings, we establish a straightforward dichotomy for the evaluation problem of positive first-order logic without equality across structures preserving multipermutions that form a monoid with a closure under inversion; specifically, these evaluation complexities are either contained within Logspace or are complete for Pspace. Finally, we investigate the full monoid of multipermutations on an n-element set under the standard relation composition operation, characterizing the associated Green's relations and regularly decomposable elements, while demonstrating that a polynomial-time generative set for monoids of size does not necessarily exist for all inputs.

The Lyncs-API functions as a Python toolkit tailored for applications in Lattice QCD. Its design aims to simplify the programming environment for running various Lattice QCD libraries from within Python, all without compromising performance across different platforms by standardizing a common software framework for these calculations. Interfaces provided include those for c-lime, DDalphaAMG, tmLQCD, and QUDA. Specifically, this paper focuses on the QUDA interface, referred to as Lyncs-QUDA, and outlines a brief tutorial on executing Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) simulations using it.

Nonlinear nanophotonics utilizes specifically engineered nanoconformations to concentrate light into minute volumes, thereby amplifying nonlinear optical effects with precise spectral and spatial manipulation. Given graphene's inherently robust, electrically tunable nonlinear response, it emerges as a leading candidate for nonlinear optoelectronic applications. This research demonstrates exceptionally robust optical nonlinearities within graphene-insulator-metal stacks, revealing a 1,000-fold increase in the third-harmonic output when compared to unmodified graphene. By adjusting the graphene Fermi energy via external gate voltages, our experiments show that graphene plasmons drive and modulate the nonlinearity, thereby regulating the third-harmonic response. Consequently, graphene-insulator-metal heterostructures are identified as a favorable architecture for developing nano-optoelectronic devices that are both optically controlled and electrically tunable.

Action Unit (AU) Detection serves as a branch of affective computing focused on identifying distinct facial muscular motions, playing a pivotal role in developing unbiased computational face representations. Consequently, it has garnered significant attention lately, although a major barrier to constructing highly efficient deep learning AU detection systems remains the scarcity of large facial image datasets annotated by AU experts. The ABAW challenge addresses this limitation and sets a new benchmark, having provided an annotated dataset comprising 2M frame-based AUs. In this paper, we introduce our submission for the ABAW3 challenge. Specifically, the method employs a multi-label transformer detector that leverages hierarchical multi-headed self-attention mechanisms to determine which specific facial regions and features in an image are crucial for detecting the relevant Action Unit.

To address the COVID-19 pandemic, an overwhelming quantity of visualizations has been developed to disseminate information to the public. For every element of this framework, we outline factors worth consideration. Finally, the paper offers recommendations to guide future investigations into crisis visualization.

Experiments utilizing pre-trained models like OpenL3, VGGish, or their combinations yielded an approach that exceeds baseline methods and enhances state-of-the-art performance in various audio classification challenges. Furthermore, empirical results highlight the advantages of feature fusion compared to utilizing isolated models in isolation.

Upon evaluation with a separate set of in-distribution chest x-rays (held out for testing), it demonstrated the potential application and robust performance across various medical imaging domains and conditions inherent in radiological practice settings where precision diagnostics matter critically today or soon.

Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) have recently become the primary focus of interest for both academia and industry. Given that AVs represent complex ecosystems comprising numerous subsystems, they frequently face significant risks, particularly from attackers. Consequently, manufacturers must regularly distribute updated firmware for these various subsystems to address bugs and add capabilities such as security patches. This study introduces a distributed firmware update framework specifically tailored to subsystems on vehicles using blockchain technology and smart contracts. To safeguard the integrity and genuineness of firmware, the solution employs a consortium blockchain involving various manufacturers. Rather than relying on a single central entity for distribution, the system empowers AVs themselves as distributors to facilitate this process, utilizing their movement to enhance deliver speed and availability through high resilience. A reward mechanism has also been introduced to encourage participation; it tracks a reputation-based credit standing for each distributor within blockchain to incentivize update sharing. To conduct the exchange of updates for distribution verification within a completely untrusting infrastructure, a zero-knowledge proof protocol is applied. In addition to this, Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) ensures strictly limited access, preventing only sanctioned AVs from downloading and utilizing latest patches. Preliminary investigations reveal that these additional cryptographic steps and transaction exchanges have no discernible impact on the network's operation, while further security assessments affirm that the proposed methodology demonstrates high resistance divers forms of cyber-attacks and secure performance.

Communications standards are currently developed through collaborative efforts where human committees convene repeatedly over extended periods until reaching an agreement, covering critical decisions like the modulation and coding techniques to be deployed over wireless links. We suggest an automated alternative for selecting these modulation and coding sets for a specific air interface, streamlining the initial design process while making it easier to future-proof standards for new services and applications with emerging high-capacity modulation methods. Our approach leverages a machine learning framework: an automated constructor entity proposes configuration sets, and an evaluator entity assigns scores in return. Through reinforcement learning, this constructor iteratively refines these proposals until it reaches a scoring threshold that reflects the jointly agreed-upon standards, encompassing necessary performance metrics for transmissions.

Standard mathematical representations of excitable cells rely on cable theory, assuming a homogenized environment and uniform spatial distributions of ionic species. Empirical evaluation confirms that PE maintain the inherent diversity found in DE while achieving comparable performance across accuracy, calibration, out-of-distribution detection, and robustness to distribution shifts.

We empirically assess the robustness of Maximum Likelihood-based uncertainty estimation techniques against outliers within training data for regression tasks. We evaluated this approach through standard regression benchmarks and a high-dimensional monocular depth estimation task, both of which contained outliers; notably, maximum likelihood models utilizing heavy-tailed distributions demonstrate enhanced estimates, effective discrimination between uncertainties in out-of-distribution data compared to benign samples under outlier presence, and improved detection of adversarial attacks within noisy training environments where clean data separation was difficult.

This research addresses the homogenization of Schrodinger equations governing non-crystalline matter, where coefficients are formed by stationary functions combined with stochastic distortions. The study derives two rigorous "effective mass theorem" results significant to solid state physics; the first presents a general abstract framework applicable beyond classical stationary ergodic conditions, while the second applies specifically to quasi-perfect materials with limited disorder.
