Time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) has become a preferred approach for computing spectral and response properties across physics, chemistry, and biology, thanks to its ability to scale efficiently, allowing the analysis of significantly larger systems. Recent applications have successfully addressed increasingly complex issues using simple functional approximations; however, there is growing recognition that these functionals can fail for many classes of problems. In this review, I outline the core challenges posed by these approximate functionals when describing specific types of transitions, notably double-excitons and charge-transfer excitations, often cited as major barriers to applying the theory reliably as a "black box." Furthermore, I discuss recent advances that have improved functional constructions to deliver more accurate results in the context of these excitations, dating across recent decades in progress in developing these function approximations.

Deep generative models, developed through machine learning training, can act as priors for solving under-determined inverse problems in imaging, specifically where data is sparse. We introduce **MrSARP**, a hierarchical deep generative model tailored for Synthetic Aperture Radiation (SAR) images, capable of synthesizing joint representations of targets at multiple resolutions simultaneously. During training, MrSARP is paired with a discriminator that evaluates combined multi-resolution outputs to ensure realism regarding the target. We detail how this architecture retrieves high-spatial-resolution images from low-resolution equivalents of the same target. Furthermore, the energy minimization objective of the generator is adjusted to enhance its efficacy in recovering original input parameters for a given set of resolution images. We assess the proposed model's performance against established super-resolution error benchmarks using simulated datasets and compare its outcomes to traditional up_sampling and sparsity-based deblurring techniques.

Direct conformational generation methods, which construct 3D structures naturally from input molecular graphs, have proven essential in various machine learning-driven molecular applications, including 3D-QSAR and drug design virtual screening. However, current approaches face challenges: their loss functions either demand excessive computational resources or fail to guarantee equivalence during optimization, unfairly penalizing certain configurations while compromising the generation of fine-grained local geometry. To address this, we introduce Equivalent Distance Geometry Error (EDGE), a metric that calculates differential discrepancy by equivalently optimizing three critical aspects of conformational geometry—namely, bond lengths, bond angles, and diatomic distances, with assigned weightings. Furthermore, an enhanced iteration minimizes the linear transformations of intra-atomic distances within a range of three hops. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that, under identical network architectures, EDGE outperforms state-of-the-art loss functions by being both highly efficacious in two specific benchmarks and significantly more time-efficient.

To tackle engineering design challenges where the solution space is too expansive for manual optimization, numerous algorithms have emerged. To streamline the creation and deployment of these methods, a Modular Optimization Framework (MOF) was established. Written in Python 3 and utilizing object-oriented programming principles, MOF employs a modular architecture that enables users to readily integrate new algorithms, methods, or engineering problems. Furthermore, a standardized input file permits users to easily define design scenarios, adjust optimization settings, and compare different algorithms. Although the present version of the MOFs includes only genetic algorithms (GA) and simulated annealing (SA), it demonstrates their utility in practical examples within various nuclear contexts. These demonstrations—covering an unconstrained nuclear fuel assembly pin lattice, a constrained first-cycle fuel loading optimization for a three-loop pressurized water reactor (PWR), and a third-cycle optimization for a four-loop PWR)—illustrate that the GA and SA implementations effectively explore solution spaces and satisfy imposed constraints. These findings not only validate the MOFs' existing tools but also offer a suite of benchmark cases for evaluating future advancements using the MOFs.

Entanglement, a phenomenon driving the rapid advances in quantum algorithms, warrants further examination within the nascent field of Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs), which have recently succeeded in simple machine learning tasks. Ultimately, while fundamental, negational symmetry is a double-edged sword that necessitates consideration within the design and application of practical quantum systems.

Modern deep neural networks frequently overfit to corrupted training sets marked by class imbalance and flawed labels, prompting the use of sample re-weighting as a common mitigation strategy. However, existing approaches often struggle in practical settings because they rely heavily on manual tuning of weighting strategies and auxiliary hyper-parameters, a process complicated by varying intra-data biases and significant effort to characterize these biases a priori. In response, this study introduces a meta-model that adaptively derives explicit, data-driven weighting schemes. By treating each class within training sets as a distinct task, this framework learns a weighting function that maps sample loss and specific task or class features directly to sample weights. Consequently, it imposes customized adjustments based on the inherent bias profiles of different classes. Comprehensive experiments using synthetic and real-world data confirm its efficacy across various biased conditions, including class imbalance, feature-independent and dependent label noise, and complex non-standard bias scenarios. Furthermore, research validates the scheme's transferability, demonstrating successful deployment of weights learned on the smaller CIFAR-10 dataset within larger systems like the full WebVision, often with significant performance gains over previous SOAT methods, eliminating the need for hyperparameter adjustment or gradient-based optimization steps. Finally, the generalized applicability of the proposed method to other domains such as robust semi-supervised learning, partial-label learning, and selective classification is also established.

Consequently, forecasting this market has long been a primary focus for research and experimentation. Short-term prediction empowers investors to achieve superior returns. Given the extreme volatility of stock prices, often influenced closely by the financial sector and news reactions, this paper explores predicting these prices using Deep Learning architectures. We assimilate news articles from various sources including technology, business, and finance to enhance our projections. Our approach progresses by first constructing a standard Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), advancing to a more complex Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) structured as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and concluding with the proposal of a FinBERT-LSTM model. Speech Translation involves converting spoken audio in one language into written text in another. Traditional cascaded systems, which combine an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) module with a Machine Translation (MT) system, struggle with error propagation. In contrast, Direct Neural Machine Translation approaches utilize a single system to eliminate this intermediate error, but they often face significant challenges due to scarcity in training data and are often applied in multi-modal scenarios like Speech Translation despite other issues. This study leverages the three-axis accelerometer embedded within PEs to address inconsistencies in step detection. We propose that (1) raw tri-axial sensor inputs can be algorithmically transformed into highly reliable and accurate step estimates, and (2) a universal counting model can efficiently adapt to distinct gait signatures using minimal subject-specific training data. Initially, an open-source repository of raw sensor readings guided the construction of a long short term memory (LSTM) deep neural network for step modeling. Subsequently, a novel dataset comprising entirely different sensors and participant groups was generated for validation. Finally, limited subject-specific data was employed via domain adaptation to generate localized models achieving superior individual accuracy. These findings indicate that models developed on vast, publicly accessible datasets remain transferable to specific patient groups where extensive historical data is scarce.

Incorporating a limiting assumption of infinite network width enables major analytic simplifications regarding the theoretical development of overparameterized neural networks. When initialized appropriately with a specific random scheme, an excessively expansive network can be closely modeled by a Gaussian process, covering the pre-trial and trial phases. This study replicates this finding for an elementary stochastic architecture where weights are treated as random variables. The closed-form computation of output distributions facilitates a PAC-Bayesian learning strategy that explicitly maximizes lower bounds on generalization error. Furthermore, empirical assessments performed on high-dimensional MNIST data demonstrate that, within a regime of large but non-infinite capacity, the novel training protocol frequently surpasses conventional PAC-Bayesian frameworks in performance.

Evaluations across multiple major language options consistently produced small but statistically significant gains in both typing velocity and decoding accuracy.

Determining semantic relationships between concepts is vital in numerous fields, where knowledge bases like ConceptNet serve as valuable resources by modeling these associations as edges within a graph. Even when direct connections are absent, conceptual relations can be approximated through the paths linking nodes. However, many such pathways are ineffective or noisy, implying that relying on path features depends entirely on the capacity to filter for high-quality trajectories. Existing systems employ basic heuristics for this selection, whereas the proposed approach leverages crowdsourced human evaluations. To achieve a universal, task-independent definition of quality, the study involves human raters ordering paths by perceived naturalness, avoiding specific guidance on what constitutes a "meaningful" indicator. Employing this data, a trained neural network accurately predicts unseen judgments, often matching human performance closely. Significantly, the experimental results demonstrate that selecting meaningful paths with this method outperforms prevailing heuristic strategies.

This article establishes pointwise theorems on martingale type convergence specifically designed for tensor product splines located in d-dimensional Euclidean space (where $d$ is a positive integer). Within these proofs, traditional conditional expectations are substituted by their corresponding tensor spline orthoprojectors. In this framework, the manuscript derives parallels to the classical martingale convergence theorem along with versions of Doob's maximal inequality, including a characterization of when a Banach space $X$ satisfies the Radon-Nikodým property based on the behavior of its pointwise $X$-valued martingales. These results maintain full consistency with standard martingale principles while holding true regardless of variations in spline degree, the specific dimension $d$, or the applied filtration structure.

We have introduced the new Stata command ldvqreg to handle quantile regression when dependent variables are binary or censored (either with upper limits, lower limits, or both). The estimators rely on a smoothed variant of the standard objective function used in this model. Simulation experiments reveal not only that it accurately estimates the necessary parameters, but also demonstrate that it should be used as a method of last resort rather than the current available procedures whenever censoring occurs within the analysis. Additionally, the approach is empirically applied to an examination of female labor force participation in Uruguay.

We introduce Human-centered 4D Scene Capture (HSC4D), a method designed to accurately and efficiently generate dynamic digital environments featuring extensive indoor-outdoor landscapes. By utilizing solely body-mounted IMUs and LiDAR, HSC4D operates in space-agnostic environments without reliance on external equipment or pre-existing digital maps. Although IMUs excel at capturing human posture yet accumulate drift during prolonged sessions, while LiDAR ensures stable global localization despite lacking precise local orientation and position details, HSC4D overcomes these limitations by jointly optimizing the strengths of both sensors, enabling robust long-term capture. Additionally, the approach explores interactions between humans and their surroundings to enhance realism. To support downstream applications such as AR, VR, robotics, and autonomous vehicles, we provide a benchmark featuring three expansive scenarios (ranging from 1,000 to 5,000 square meters) that accurately represent dynamic human locations and movements across varied settings like gyms, multi-story buildings, and slopes. Activities including exercise, stair negotiation, and climbing are included to validate the system's comprehensive effectiveness and generalizability. Resources, including the full dataset and implementation code, are hosted at http://www.lidarhumanmotion.net/hsc4d/.

We present end-to-end jet image classifiers constructed from simulated low-level detector information using high-fideltity CMS Open Data, designed to distinguish quark-initiated from gluon-initiated jets. Our analysis emphasizes the critical role of precise spatial details and achieves performance commensurate with current state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we expand this end-to-end strategy for event-level quark-gluon di-jet QCD discrimination. When contrasted with methods utilizing hand-engineered features, the fully automated end-to-end algorithm exhibits strong resilience against background noise arising from the underlying event and pile-up.

Our study demonstrates that spin-orbit coupling exhibits a dual role in driving orbitally-selective Mott transitions within the minimal ruthenate-model of a crystal-field-split, three-orbital Hubbard model at $2/3$ filling. Specifically, spin-orbit coupling promotes metallicity by enhancing orbital hybridization at low interaction strengths, whereas at high interaction strengths, it supports a Mott insulating state through the removal of orbital degeneracies and the increase of band polarizations. An intermediate phase of orbitally-selective non-Fermi liquid (OSnFL) emerges, characterized by the simultaneous persistence and failure of Fermi-liquid behavior across different orbitals; this exotic phase, potentially mediated by an orbitally-selective Kondo mechanism, offers an explanation for the unique metallic properties observed under various strain and pressure conditions in 4$d$ compounds such as Ca$_{1.8}$Sr$_{0.2}$RuO$_4$, Ba$_2$RuO$_4$, and Sr$_2$RuO$_4$.

This paper introduces a Partial Least Squares (PLS) approach designed to estimate the multiple-function-on-function regression model that incorporates a single functional response alongside quadratic, interaction effects with multiple functional predictors. While the direct estimation of such models is notoriously ill-posed due to their infinite-dimensional nature, the standard practical approach projects the functional data into a finite-dimensional basis function subspace. Specifically, the functional coefficients are approximated by expanding functional variables into a finite basis; consequently, the model transforms into a conventional multivariate regression. The proposed PLS framework reformulates the problem to account for a single functional response, a weighted combination of multiple functional predictors utilizing quadratic/interaction terms, or equivalently, the resulting basis expansions. This paper demonstrates the theoretical equivalence between these two formulations. Building on PLS derived from basis expansions, we derive a closed-form algorithm yielding the coefficient functions in terms of functional data. Given the uncertainty inherent in determining true model specifications, a specific forward selection procedure is proposed for model determination. The method's effectiveness is evaluated through multiple Monte Carlo simulations alongside two empirical case studies. The findings indicate that this novel approach generates results comparable to, or potentially superior to, established existing methods within a finite-sample framework.

Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), a nonparametric method for the two-sample problem, typically employs a witness function—a real-valued kernel-based weighted sum—with the testestimates defining its expectation and structure. Standard practice tunes the witness via a held-out task (selective testing) to maintain robust control. Here are the new findings. We present an improved test that defines the witness basing on testestimates for higher test power and efficiency. We present several conclusions: (1) the new test is consistent in detecting differences and maintains control with a well-controlled type I error; (2) the maximum-likelihood witness can be represented as the average of the data in kernel, where each data is a multiple of the weight in the feature; (3) the proposed test power compares is superior or indistinguishable from classical tests when adjusted to correct the data (empirical validation is performed on datasets including the Higgs benchmark dataset).

Although the dynamical structure factor is a critical observable for quantum magnetism, numerically and theoretically predicting it in Hubbard-like models outside of one dimension has proven difficult to achieve. This study investigates the magnetic excitations in the triangular lattice Hubbard model involving next-nearest neighbor hopping, deriving magneton spectra through a self-consistent random phase approximation initiated from stripe and $120^{\circ}$ magnetic ordering states. Across system parameters, we discover generic accidental zero modes originating from a well-established classical degeneracy present in the corresponding $J$–$J$ Heisenberg model; notably when employing the stripe state order. We broaden our understanding by highlighting that the "order-by-disorders" concept applies to Hubbard systems and illustrate the mechanism via which quantum fluctuations stabilize the stripe state of matter that occurs. Moreover the condense phase formed as result from frustration enables us to completely define an energy landscape of condensed matter behavior with quantum fluctuations described by Hubbard lattice models, showing remarkable agreement with previous research in the numerical analysis field. Finally, we examine connections with experimental findings for various realizations of triangular geometry systems and additionally our proposed connection between theoretical observations and cholestic spin states within this system.

For smart contract applications to fully realize their potential on the blockchain, they must integrate smoothly with legacy software through an appropriate programmatic interface. Such an interface needs to support contract initiation, execution, and the ability to query the current state of the chain. We propose and define a typed abstract programming interface (API) that enables us to formally prove safety properties within the combined system model. Specifically, our analysis yields execution semantics ensuring type-safe communication between external programs and the blockchain. These properties also underpin the design constraints for the interface. We have implemented an experimental version of this system in OCaml designed for the Tezos platform.

This paper introduces an artificial intelligence system designed to predict microsatellite instability (MSI) from colorectal carcinoma Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) slides processed on Tissue Microarrays (TMAs) using specialized Deep Learning architectures. Our workflow utilizes an end-to-end preprocessing pipeline capable of generating multi-magnification image tiles within regions of interest identified by an upstream tissue classification guide and filtered through one module that targets multiple batch biases. Datasets used for training and validation were sourced primarily from the extensive biological collection provided by EPICOLON and augmented with samples derived from a specific single-institution cohort. Through a comprehensive assessment of statistical disparities, researchers recognized three specific confounders correlated with baseline DL learned features: the sample provider, unique patient biopsy spot, and specific physical glass slide location. To mitigate these influences, an adversarially trained, multi-bias rejection component was embedded into the neural network to prevent its incorporation of such batch-specific variables during representation learning. Results indicate that these optimized, debiased representations possess superior discriminatory ability regarding the MSI detection task while exhibiting minimal statistical dependency on redundant bias variables and low statistical agreement with known biases. Our experimental design scrutinized the influence of variable tissue regions, imaging scales, and diagnostic performance ranging from pixel-level tiles to final pathology reports (AUC). The system consistently achieved Tile AUC results around 0.87 when evaluating three included tissue phenotypes—mucin, tumor epithelium, lymphocytic infiltrate—across four focus magnitudes, rising slightly after aggregating predictions to patient-level granularity to 0.90 across tumor cells. Ultimately, this study constitutes a pioneering integration of multiple bias elimination techniques within the digital pathology-specific deep learning framework for predicting MSI status from TMAs, representing its first application to this domain.

Perfusion imaging represents a promising method for evaluating liver cancer treatment outcomes. The C-Arm CT offers a distinct advantage for performing these perfusion assessments intra-operatively, allowing even quicker evaluation; however, limitations due to the system's gradual rotation and high noise levels affect reconstruction quality. To mitigate these challenges, model-based approaches have gained traction. This research implements Time Separation Technique (TST), utilizing this method to suppress noisy artifacts in the raw data, accelerate the image reconstruction, and enhance final perfusion image quality. Utilizing data from in-vivo animal experiments demonstrates that Dynamic C-Arm CT Liver Perfusion Imaging, when coupled with TST-based data processing, yield results that hold strong comparability to the Gold-Standard of conventional CT perfusion.

For years, support schemes such as Feed-in-Tariffs (FiT) have significantly encouraged the adoption of distributed energy resources and fueled the shift toward a prosumer-focused model driven by system democratization and decarbonization. While this transformation offers both challenges and opportunities to grid operators and fosters new innovations like local energy markets, the assumption often held that FiTs represented the minimum economic incentive for prosumer participation is becoming outdated as the regime is being retired across several nations. Consequently, this study introduces a novel pricing mechanism anchored to the Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE), aimed at ensuring prosumer profitability while establishing a price structure that is both transparent and equitable for all stakeholders. Developed within a Distributed Ledger Technology framework and adopting a Cyber-Physical-Social-System perspective as the market architecture, the proposed approach was rigorously evaluated against conventional FiT and other current transition strategies through various fixed and variable contract models. Findings indicate that while consumer savings rise compared to the old FiT model resulting in slightly diminished prosumer revenue, a direct comparison with currently suggested FiT replacements reveals that this proposed mechanism delivers substantial net gains for the entire ecosystem.

We detail an extensive analysis of Galactic black hole transient GRS 1716-249 throughout its 2016-2017 eruption, covering observations across optical (Las Cumbres Observatory), ultraviolet (Swift Observatory Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope), near-infrared (Rapid Eye Mountain telescope) and mid-infrared (Very Large Telescope) wavelengths, complemented by archived X-ray and radio data. Our results indicate that the optical/ near-infrared and UV radiation primarily stems from a multi-temperature accretion disk, whereas mid-infrared and radio emissions are driven by synchrotron radiation from a compact jet. The X-ray flux in the hard state shows a correlation with the optical/UV luminosity, supporting a model where the optical/UV emission is an interplay between viscous heating and X-ray irradiation as the outburst wanes. Additionally, presenting a long-term optical light curve, this study determines a quiescent i-band magnitude of 21.39±0.13. Crucially, because past determinations of system parameters relied on flawed premises and thus likely remain inaccurate, this new analysis argues in favor of revisiting established metrics by contrasting current data against outbursting black hole X-ray binary systems. While GRG 1716-249 exhibits X-ray behavior similar to others (given the 2.4 kpc distance assumed in literature), it appears optically dim; therefore, through multiple reasoning approaches and comparisons, this suggests its true distance exceeds previously accepted values, most reasonably ranging from approximately 4 to 8 kpc.

While prior studies have demonstrated the vulnerability of 3D point cloud classifiers to adversarial attacks, most existing techniques focus on white-box scenarios by assuming the attack model has full knowledge of the target's architecture and parameters, which is unrealistic for real-world scenarios. To enhance black-box attack effectiveness, the research field typically resorts to transfer-based attacks, yet the transferability current 3D adversarial methods achieve remains limited. To address this, our paper introduces the "Scale and Shear" (SS) Attack to produce highly transferable adversarial 3D instances by randomly amplifying or skewing the input point clouds. This prevents overfitting the specific white-box source model used during training, thus increasing overall transferability. This overview evaluates a extensive assortment of open-source solutions within the quantum computing ecosystem, addressing the complete software pipeline—ranging from hardware interfaces to compilers and algorithm implementations—across various paradigms such as quantum annealing, and discrete and continuous-variable gate-based systems. Each entry is assessed on technical documentation, licensing terms, programming languages used, adherence to software engineering standards, and the host community's culture. Analysis reveals that while the variety of available projects is impressive, only a limited number successfully engage external contributors, and several major industry-backed tools exhibit notable deficiencies in software craftsmanship. Consequently, the article identifies best practices essential for cultivating an active quantum software community; this involves creating an accessible environment for new practitioners while maintaining standards that ensure high quality and thorough documentation.

Active learning efficiently collects training data instances for deep learning models, particularly in scenarios involving high annotation costs and scarce labeled datasets. While data augmentation serves as an effective remedy for expanding limited labeled instances, the potential contribution of these augmented "virtual" instances within the active learning selection mechanism has remained unaddressed. To bridge the gap between acquisition and augmentation, this paper introduces LADALOOK-AHEAD Data Acquisition, or LADA—a framework that integrates both processes. Unlike prior approaches selecting only from unlabeled data in isolation, LADA simultaneously pre-decides both which real unlabeled instances to acquire from existing data sources, then which virtual instances will synthesize them, explicitly optimizing them for informativeness through InfoMixUp and InfoSTN by leveraging maximum predictive acquisition scores. To demonstrate the robustness of LADALOOK-AHEAD Data Acquisition as a generalized structure, we evaluated different method pairisons against various benchmarks incorporating both techniques distinctly; results show significant improvements surpass current baselines.

Reinforcement learning environments often lack standardized conventions for structuring action spaces; as a result, applying RL algorithms to tasks involving large, multi-part action spaces demands additional customization efforts to align with varying formats. Economic Model Predictive Control (EMPC) and Tracking Model Predictive Control (TMPC) are two prevalent advanced control schemes applied across many domains. Notably, this approach supports pre-configuring boundary offsets ("back-off") and shifting targets to ensure controlled process robustness. Broad simulations across varied scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method offers valuable insights for performance assessment and controller synthesis.

Dynamic simulations of microbial metabolism typically apply flux balance analysis under a quasi-steady state, requiring costly optimization calculations for every species at every time step. When feaibility begins to wane, a complementary but related optimization selects a new appropriate flux basis for continued forward progression. Our algorithm was prototyped in Python.

Spin glasses are notoriously challenging for analytical and numerical investigation, largely because of frustration-induced metastability and highly rugged, non-convexc energy landscapes that necessitate collective updates for efficient exploration. Current algorithms depend on stochastic clusters to execute non-local shifts, yet these "cluster algorithms" often lack universal efficiency. In this study, we propose an out-of-equilibrium framework for spinning-glass simulations based on classical dynamics incorporating memory mechanisms. Simulations across multiple types of ³D spin glasses—specifically Edwards-Anderson, partially-faultersated, and fully-favored variants—reveal that memory dynamically fosters critical spin clusters during temporal evolution through self-organizing processes, enabling a more efficient traversal of the low-temperature regimes characteristic of spin-glasses.

The interest in high-entropy alloy thermoelectric materials relies on the expectation of minimizing $\tableof\ll$ by introducing significant compositional disorder. However, our results show that when considering a specific mechanism like mass-contrast phonon scattering, $\tableof\ll$ reaches its minimum at the binary system exhibiting the greatest mass disparity; consequently, incorporating intermediate-mass atoms solely to increase disorder may inadvertently raise thermal conductivity. Improvement only occurs if every component introduces a distinct scattering mechanism—for instance, combining mass fluctuations with strain variations. Moreover, known interactions of alloying induce scattering in both heat-transport phonons and charge carriers, creating a fundamental trade-off for thermoelectric efficiency. We utilize analytical transport models rooted in effective medium and perturbation theories to forecast how alloy impact modifies thermal and electronic transport properties across complete compositional ranges within several pseudo-ternary and pseudo-quaternary systems. Specifically, we present multi-component adaptations to binary alloy models for both phenomena using virtual crystal approximations. Finally, we demonstrate that standard functional forms from computational thermodynamics can extend these models to further characterize scattering behavior.

Drawing upon the principles of compressive sensing, we introduce an unconventional approach to error control in digital communication by embedding data within both the support vector and the non-zero elements of a sparse sequence. By constructing a codeword that results from the multiplication of this sparse sequence against a tailored dictionary matrix—specifically, via the sparse and unweighted summing of its column vectors, transmission is facilitated. The receiver utilizes adaptations of iterative sparse reconstruction techniques to identify the original data. This system leverages specific mathematical dictionary sources based on quantum information theory principles, particularly orthogonal bases often employed in telecommunications and quantum frameworks, to evaluate its reliability through Block Error Rate metrics under Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN). Extensive results show the method achieving parity and superior efficiency compared with common linear codes, particularly advantageous in environments of limited block length. Furthermore, our scheme displays inherent adaptability for multi-access scenarios like broadcasting and interfering networks by organizing user nodes. This performance equivalence in multi-access settings is contingent upon user stratifications; when a system's users share analogous noise susceptibilities and thermal gain profiles, our architecture converges reliably with single-user standards. The proposed approach naturally extends beyond single-user contexts to multiple-access scenarios such as multi-channel access, multicast transmission, and shared interference channels, effectively maintaining single-user equivalent performance under specific system constraints.

ViDaExpert serves as a specialized utility for the visualization and analysis of multidimensional vectorial datasets. Designed to handle "object-feature" formatted tables—controlling both numerical attributes and textual row/column labels—it integrates a suite of statistical techniques, including standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Elastic Maps (offering a non-linear approach to PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) and multilinear regression, alongside K-Means clustering and decision-tree construction variants. Featuring an array of intuitive dialogs for configuring data point properties such as size, shape, and color, along with rapid 3D rendering capabilities, ViDa Expert functions as a powerful instrument. This enables users to generate interactive 3D scenes representing high-dimensional data tables while efficiently executing both foundational and sophisticated statistical analyses.

How do we identify anomalies, specifically samples that substantially deviate from high-dimensional data clusters such as images or sensor readings? This challenge is both theoretically significant for enhancing the robustness of learning algorithms against unexpected inputs and practically valuable across many domains. Autoencoders represent a prevalent solution owing to their modular architecture and capacity to compress dimensionality; yet, the standard anomaly scoring mechanism struggles with these capabilities because the inherent fluctuation of reconstruction error among legitimate samples undermines accurate detection. Experiments with empirical real-world data highlight that adapting anomaly scoring to local conditions is paramount. Consequently, we present a novel Adaptive Reconstruction Error-based Scoring method, which adjusts its evaluation metrics according to the localization behavior of reconstruction error within the latent space. Our results demonstrate that this technique yields superior anomaly detection performance compared to relevant baseline models across a extensive selection of benchmark datasets.

During the NeurIPS 2022-hosted Weather4Cast competition, which demanded the prediction of super-resolution precipitation movies across diverse European zones given low-resolution, wide-area satellite inputs, we demonstrate that a general-purpose 3D U-Net baseline achieves significant enhancements through the integration of region-conditioned layers and 1x1x1 orthographic regularization. Furthermore, we promote robust generalization via an ensemble of strategies including mixup data augmentation, self-distillation, and feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). These adaptations yield performance improvements of up to 19.54% over standard 3D U-Net models with fewer than 1% additional parameters, culminating in fourth-place finishes on the core leaderboards.

This study investigates the $\gamma p \to K^+ K^- p$ reaction by employing the generalized Veneziano ($B_5$) model within the framework of double Regge exchange. We simulated four distinct configurations based on the various signature combinations of the dominant Regge exchanges: ($K^*,a_2/f_2$), ($K^*,\rho/\omega$), ($K_2^*,a_2/f_2$), and ($K_2^*,\rho/\omega$), utilizing a Monte Carlo approach. To effectively isolate appropriate event candidates suitable for the high-energy double Regge exchange limit, we prioritized \textit{Van Hove} plots over conventional kinematical restrictions applied to the $K^+ K^- p$ Dalitz plot. This strategy enables us to predict and examine the specific double Regge contribution manifest in the $K^+ K^- p$ Dalitz distribution. This analysis is crucial, as this component represents a primary background when researching strangeonia, hybrids, and exotics via the $\gamma p\to K^+K^-p$ channel. We anticipate that current data, along with forthcoming results, will facilitate verification of the proposed double Regge dynamics and allow for a refined evaluation of the relevant part of the interaction's amplitude.

The orientation and character of electron orbitals within the momentum manifold, termed orbital texture, plays a pivotal role in the onset of collective phases that break symmetry, including superconductors, topological matter, and charge density waves. We investigated this phenomenon in the metal dichalcogenide 1T-TiTe$_2$ by conducting extreme ultraviolet angular-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (nano-ARPES) on crystals aligned along two opposite mirror-symmetry directions, allowing for the specific identification of how orbital textures influence photoemission. By correlating these experimental findings with calculations using quantitative one-step models of the photoemission process alongside intuitive density-based tight-binding frameworks, we explicitly confirm that variations in the momentum orientation of the orbitals cause strong linear dichroism in photoelectron patterns. Consequently, our findings mark a crucial advancement beyond conventional band-structure visualization, enabling the exploration of the electronic orbital textures and wavefunctions through the utilization of matrix-element effects in spectroscopy.

Conventional supervised learning fundamentally assumes that test samples follow the same distribution as training samples, a condition known as closed-set classification. This assumption frequently breaks down in real-world scenarios where the test set contains unseen or unknown classes; this situation is termed the open-set scenario, which highlights open-set detection needs, a task that is vital in high-stakes, safety-critical applications. We address the open-set recognition challenge—identifying these unseen specimens—by leveraging learned pairwise similarities. Our approach follows a dual-step process: first, a闭 set classifier (using data from known classes) is trained, and subsequently, the system learns the metric for distinguishing known classes from synthetic unseen instances. To create these synthetic unseen-like anomalies, we apply augmentation techniques that induce distribution shifting on existing training samples, generating pseudo-unseen exemplars. We designate this approach as OPG (**R**ecognition based on **Pseudo** unseen **-** generated data. Our evaluation demonstrates that these learned multi-feature baselines achieve an accurate distinction between familiar novel classes on established benchmarks designed for open-set testing and open-set tasks.

Incompressible non-Abelian topological fluids known as the Pfaffian fractional quantum Hall (FQH) state exist within a half-filled electronic Landau level with equal densities of electrons and holes, producing half-integral quantum Hall transitions that bridge integer FQH states. Conversely, Abelian fractional quantum phases, exemplifying the Laughlin state, have been analyzed using partons regarded as fermionic subunits of electrons. In this study, we introduce a novel class of paired parton FQH states occurring at filling factors \(\nu=1/3, -1/3, \ldots\), appearing at critical interfaces between integer FQH states and standard Abelian states that typically fill \(\nu=1/3\). Like the Pfaffian electronic state, these paired partons arise from a balanced population in a partonic half-level. Federated Learning (FL) has become prominent for empowering large-scale, privacy-focused machine learning, but frequent gradient synchronization creates substantial communication burdens that hinder FL performance. Existing mitigation strategies focus on (i) locally updating model weights—which balances computation and communication—and (ii) compressing gradients, which balances precision and communication. Despite the significant performance potential, jointly and dynamically optimizing both trade-offs to address convergence impacts remains an unresolved challenge. In this work, we formulate the objective to minimize error by directly optimizing two parameters: local update rates and gradient sparsity thresholds, which govern the computation-communication and precision-communication trade-offs, respectively. By deriving an upper bound for learning accuracy within specific execution time windows and analyzing the correlation between these variables, we introduce Fast FL (FFL), a method that dynamically tunes both factors simultaneously. Experiments confirm that our approach outperforms existing schemes, achieving superior accuracy more efficiently.

Modeling diffusion on evolving contact networks is a critical field for epidemiology, marketing, cybersecurity, and ecology. Nevertheless, existing models fail to account transmissions from indirect interactions. Specifically, cases arise where an infectious individual releases particles that linger in the air, enabling transmission to susceptible individuals who arrive after the infected source has departed; consequently, current models overlook these events. To address this, this thesis introduces the same-place-different-time (SPDT) transmission diffusion model. Analysis applied to real dynamic contact network datasets reveals that SPDT leads to pronounced amplifications in diffusion dynamics and exhibits novel behaviors distinct from traditional approaches to supplement diffusion. Additionally, we enhance shape and pose comprehension by refining a pretrained, off-the-shelf vision transformer model and injecting its latent features. Text generation plays a critical role in diverse natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, standard decoding algorithms relying on maximization, such as beam search in neural language models, frequently produce degenerate outputs characterized as unnatural text rife with unwanted repetitions. Although existing techniques mitigate this issue by injecting randomness through sampling techniques or altering training targets to lower token scores like in unlikelihood training (UITL), they often fail to maintain semantic cohesion. To address this, we propose a contrastive approach featuring two main components: SimCTG, which serves as a contrastive objective to refine the model's internal representation space for diversity, thereby fostering variety while preserving coherence. The study concludes with strategic recommendations targeted at various stakeholders—including industry practitioners, developers, researchers, educators, and policy regulators—to foster a more global and effective framework for securing software.

The surge in data volumes and the growing need for instant, recent-data analysis have spawned hybrid Transactional and Analytical Processing (HTAP) databases capable of executing both operations simultaneously, eliminating expensive synchronization between disconnected single-use systems. However, when handling high-frequency updates, leading HTAP architectures suffer substantial performance drops in transactional (up to 74.6%) and analytical (up to 49.8%) workloads compared to using specialized systems independently. This inefficiency stems from CPU-to-memory transfers, state updates across workloads, and the overhead of ensuring system-wide data consistency. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Polynesia, a co-design solution for HTAP databases stored directly in RAM, engineered to bypass typical throughput penalties by (1) isolating transactional and analytical tasks within separate processing environments, (2) deploying specialized hardware that facilitates software optimizations for lower consistency and update costs, and (3) leveraging processing-in-memory for analytical modules to minimize memory movement overheads. Evaluations demonstrate that Polynesia surpasses three state-of-the-art HTAP systems by achieving average throughput gains of 1.7x for transactions and 3.7x for analysis while cutting energy usage by 48% relative to the previous best-low-power contender.

Accurate and computationally efficient assessment of Newtonian potentials across diverse two-dimensional regions is vital for the numerical solution of Poisson equations and volume integral equations. For intricate shapes, discretization via unstructured grids makes direct potential calculation using quadrature prohibitively expensive. This study proposes a straightforward yet efficient high-order scheme for determining these potentials by employing Green's third identity to convert volume integrals into boundary forms that are well-suited for the Helsing-Ojala method. Consequently, the traditionally heavy computation time required for self-interaction and nearfield evaluations on unstructured grids becomes approximately equal to that of farfield interaction calculations handled by the Fast Multipole Method (FMM). A cornerstone of this algorithm is a high-order monomial approximation of functions within mesh elements; although often regarded as poorly conditioned due to the need to solve Vandermonde systems involving smooth function expansions, our analysis demonstrates that with a backward stable solver, this approach can achieve uniform high accuracy. We provide a rigorous foundation for this long-standung observation, with numerical results validating the algorithm's efficacy.

For temporal modeling, an initial entropic analysis filters out the most stable historical sequences, followed by integrated correlation-Fourier analysis to ascertain regular cycles, thereby forming a temporal matrix. These matrices are integrated into a customized, low-rank tensor learning completion problem. Beyond mere answer prediction, increasing tasks in Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) demand the additional extraction of evidence sentences to support those answers; however, annotating these evidential sentences typically proves laborious and time-consuming. Creating extensive hydrodynamical simulations required for future cosmological observations places immense demands on computing resources. Forecasting the next movements of vehicles, cyclists, and other participants is a pivotal requirement for autonomous driving systems. Notably, FJMP secured the first place on the INTERACTION dataset’s multi-agent evaluation benchmark.

The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem and Edit Distance have been investigated thoroughly for numerous years. For exact solutions involving character insertions and deletions, these problems are equivalent, achieving near-quadratic runtime, which is currently optimal according to plausible fine-grained complexity conjectures. In the realm of approximation algorithms, however, an alternative landscape exists: Edit Distance algorithms see a history of increasingly improved bounds, whereas LCS for binary strings was historically limited to a mere $1/2$-approximation. Social media platforms shape online behavior by curating content based heavily on users' past interests, effectively trapping them in "filter bubbles" that severely restrict exposure to alternative ideas. This study examines such dynamics using a multistate voter model, in which users, with probability $\lambda$, receive algorithmic guidance toward opinions prevalent in their own history. Our analysis reveals a critical transition: for low values of $\lambda$, consensus emerges, but beyond a critical threshold ($\lambda_c$), the system polarizes, causing distinct opinion clusters to persist permanently regardless of time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this critical threshold vanishes as system size $N$ increases toward zero, implying that achieving total consensus becomes virtually unattainable within massive networks due to intense polarization. This insight underscores potential dangers associated with the expansion of personalization algorithms across the web.

As a continuation of a three-part series, our results establish an analogue to the correspondence that relates the number of genus $g$ curves within a prescribed linear system of an abelian surface to a corresponding tropical count. This connection relies on associating linear systems governed by complex curves with specific integrals of 1-forms computed over cycles residing on these curves. Subsequently, we present both the expression for tropical multiplicity derived from this analogue theorem and a rigorous proof demonstrating that multiplicity remains invariant. By doing so, we introduce refined Block-Göttsch type invariants defined for abelian surfaces.

While recent learning-based techniques can estimate both extrinsic and intrinsic camera parameters directly from a single image, their performance suffers on fisheye images due to discrepancies between the expected and actual projection models. We address this limitation by introducing a versatile camera model capable of accommodating different distortion types. This generic model integrates with existing learning-based pipelines through an efficient, closed-form numerical computation for camera projection. Along with this framework, we introduce a specific calibration method designed to jointly optimize rotation and fisheye distortion. We also propose a specialized loss function that reduces magnitude bias across the four extrinsic and intrinsic parameters evaluated. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods on two large-scale datasets as well as images captured by commercial off-the-shelf fisheye cameras. Notably, we represent the first research effort to systematically analyze learning-based performance across varied projection models tailored for commercial devices in this domain.

Moire patterns in two-dimensional stacks arise either from twisting one sheet slightly relative to another or from the lattice misregistry inherent in heterostructures. This research introduces a continuous model describing the elastic energy of such moiré systems, encompassing both intra-layer stress and interlayer mismatch energy, which reaches its minimum in two distinct stacking configurations. Through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulation, we demonstrate that minimizing global elastic energy under specified boundary constraints produces extended alternating zones of one preferred stacking arrangement, interrupted by domain boundaries. Building upon the bilayer continuum model, we derive specific characteristics of these domain walls and provide a rigorous asymptotic estimate of their structure for layered moiré systems. Additionally, regarding strictly moiré unit cells in twisted geometries, we refine the $L_2$-gradient norm bound, establishing a scaling that decreases or remains at inverse linearity with increasing twist angle. This result aligns with observations of one-dimensional domain walls maintaining fixed dimensions around triangular domains at exceedingly low twist angles.
